H0430H.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily designates the unique God of the patriarchs and of Israel, the one who makes covenants and liberates His people. It also appears for the false gods or idols that nations worship, and can even qualify judges or human authorities (Exodus 21:6, for example). The context always determines whether it refers to the true God or to a human or fictitious deity. In Genesis 33:20, Jacob confesses his faith by building an altar to the God of Israel, expressing his gratitude to the one who guided and protected him throughout his exile and return.
H0430H.portee: For the Christian, this word anchors faith in a real, living, and powerful God, who is not an abstract idea but a Being who acts. It reminds us that God is a force with which one does not joke, to whom respect and obedience are due. Recognizing the unique God means rejecting false gods and false authorities that claim to dominate us. It is also to entrust one's life to the one who has the power to create, to judge, and to save.

sens: Location in Palestine, in the mountainous region, where prophets gathered
H0430I.detail: 1. This name designates a specific geographical place: a hill (or "Gibeah") in ancient Israel. The term "God" means "God" in Hebrew, so the full name literally means "the Gibeah of God" or "the Gibeah of Elohim." It is a place associated with prophetic life and the divine presence among the people.
H0430I.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "Gibeah" (Hebrew giv'ah, גִּבְעָה) means "hill" or "height," and "Elohim" (אֱלֹהִים) means "God." In ancient Hebrew, places were often named based on their physical geography or their religious significance. The name "Gibeah of God" suggests that it was a hill dedicated to spiritual life, particularly to the ministry of prophets.
H0430I.emploi: This place appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 10:5, in the account of Saul's life. Samuel sends Saul there after anointing him king, announcing to him that he will meet a company of prophets coming down from a height, equipped with musical instruments and prophesying. It is there that the Spirit of God is to come upon Saul in a visible and transformative way. The place is thus presented as a center of prophetic and spiritual life, a location where the presence of God is manifested in a particular way.
H0430I.portee: This passage reminds us that God establishes places and communities where His presence becomes visible, particularly through the prophetic gift. For the believer, it shows that God can transform a person — here Saul — through a true encounter with His Spirit, and that spiritual life is not solitary but communal.

sens: A particle that draws attention to what has just appeared
Marks astonishment or admiration in front of a sudden vision
Introduces an important revelation or discovery
H0431.detail:
1. This interjection serves to point out, to stop the reader's gaze on something that has emerged or that has just been discovered. It's like shouting "Look!" or "Attention!" — the speaker wants their interlocutor to immediately see what is manifesting. In Daniel 4:10, the dreamer says, "here, there was in the midst of the earth a tree": he has just seen the tree appear in his vision and urgently signals it to us.
2. It often accompanies a vision or an appearance that astonishes or strikes the mind. In Daniel 7:8, the prophet scrutinizes the horns and then exclaims, "here, another little horn came up" — it is the very moment he discovers something unexpected and communicates it forcefully.
3. It prepares the reader to receive something important or revealing: an image, a word, an event that makes sense. Daniel's visions are filled with this, as these images contain mysteries to decipher.
H0431.origine: This word comes from Aramaic, the language spoken by the Jews after the exile in Babylon. It is related to the ancient Hebrew "woe!" (אַלְלַי, allaï), an older exclamation. The word has retained its force as an interjection: it is a cry from the heart, a word that springs forth to point something out.
H0431.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, all in the book of Daniel, and always in the context of prophetic visions. Daniel uses it to mark key moments in his dreams: when the giant tree appears to him (4:10), when a holy being descends from heaven (4:13), when a mysterious horn grows among the others (7:8). The Segond translates it sometimes as "here," sometimes as "see" — two renderings of the same cry, as the word first invites one to look, to truly see what is being shown.
H0431.portee: For the believer, this simple interjection reminds us that God often speaks through images that require keen attention and an open heart. When Daniel says "here," he invites us to slow down, to fix our gaze, to welcome what God wants to reveal to us. It is a lesson in spiritual vigilance: not to let the signs that God gives us pass by, but to contemplate them, meditate on them, understand them.

sens: A condition presented as contrary to the facts, introducing an unreal or impossible supposition
A hypothesis formulated only for the sake of form, knowing that it will not come true
H0432.detail: 1. This word expresses a condition that does not correspond to reality: it introduces a supposition contrary to real facts. In Esther 7:4, Esther says, "if we had been sold only to become slaves," but that is not the case — they want to destroy them. She evokes a less grave hypothesis, just to show that even in this less dire scenario, she would have endured; but since it is much worse, she cries out. 2. This type of condition expresses a thought like "even if that were true (which it is not)," to better highlight the contrast with reality. In Ecclesiastes 6:6, the author says, "if that man were to live two thousand years," which is humanly impossible, to emphasize that the length of life without happiness changes nothing: the unrealistic hypothesis measures the absurdity of the real case.
H0432.origine: The Hebrew word אִלּוּ (illu) comes from the realm of Hebrew conditionals. It specifically expresses a hypothesis contrary to the facts, different from simple ordinary "if". It is a common thought structure in Hebrew to express the unreal or impossible, allowing the speaker to explore a fictional scenario to draw a conclusion about reality.
H0432.emploi: This word appears twice in the provided Hebrew Bible: in Esther 7:4, where Esther uses it to plead her case before the king by posing a fictitious hypothesis (being reduced to slavery, which would be less grave than the threat of extermination), and in Ecclesiastes 6:6, where the Preacher uses it to express an impossibility (living two thousand years) in order to highlight the absurdity of existence without enjoyment. In both cases, it is an unreal condition: it is never presented as true, but as a rhetorical device to illuminate the real situation.
H0432.portee: This word shows us how the Bible expresses reasoning and argumentation: by formulating an impossible or contrary-to-fact hypothesis, one can shed light on the absurdity or injustice of a real situation. It also illustrates how biblical authors think and speak to convince: by playing on the contrast between the fictional scenario and the painful reality.

sens: The living and true God, creator and sovereign of heaven and earth
A false god, an idol, an object of human worship other than the true God
H0433.detail:
1. This word primarily designates the true God, the one who truly exists, who created the universe and governs all things. It is used to speak of His power, justice, and majesty. For example, Job asks to be weighed by God in just balances (Job 31:6), acknowledging His authority to judge the integrity of men.
2. The word can also refer to a false god, that is, a deity that humans construct or worship in place of the true God. Job notes that some "make a god of their strength" (Job 12:6), turning their own power into an object of worship. Similarly, Habakkuk mentions one who "makes a god of his net" (Habakkuk 1:11), worshiping the means of his success rather than God Himself.
H0433.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses power and authority. It is close to the Aramaic word elah (אֱלָהּ), used in the Aramaic parts of the Bible (Daniel). The word belongs to an ancient family of terms designating divinity in Semitic languages, and it emphasizes God as the supreme power to whom all authority belongs.
H0433.emploi: This word appears about 56 times in biblical Hebrew, especially in wisdom literature like Job and the Psalms. In Job, it is very frequent: Job speaks of God who tests him, judges him, accuses him, or comforts him. The Psalms use it to express God's majesty and incomparability: "Who is God, except the Lord?" (Psalms 18:32). In historical books, it serves to describe the abandonment of God or the refusal to acknowledge Him. The word can designate either the true God with reverence or false gods with a tone of reproach or irony.
H0433.portee: This word reminds the believer that God alone is worthy of worship and absolute trust. It invites us to examine what we truly worship — our strength, our wealth, our wisdom — and to redirect our hearts toward God Himself. It is an invitation to religious sincerity: not to invent comfortable gods for ourselves, but to submit to the living and true God.

sens: The sixth month of the Jewish calendar, corresponding to August-September of our current calendar
H0435.detail: 1. Elul is the name of the sixth month of the Jewish year. It is an autumn month that corresponds approximately to August or September in our modern calendar. In the account of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile, Nehemiah tells us that the wall was completed on the 25th day of the month of Elul (Nehemiah 6:15), thus marking a crucial milestone in the restoration of God's people.
H0435.origine: The Hebrew word Elul comes from a root that evokes "absence" or "nothingness." It is a term borrowed from the Babylonian calendar during the Jewish exile in Babylon. The Jews retained this month name upon returning to Jerusalem, and it has remained the official name of the sixth month of the Hebrew calendar still used today.
H0435.emploi: Elul appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. The context is that of the restoration of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, after the Babylonian exile. Its mention specifies the exact moment when the gates of the rebuilt wall were completed and set in place, highlighting the importance of this date in the chronology of the renovation of the people and the temple.

sens: a large tree with strong branches and hard wood
a recognizable place where people gathered
a location associated with religious practices or divination
H0436G.detail: 1. The oak is a large, robust tree, very common in the Holy Land, that can live for a very long time and whose wood is hard and valuable. It is an impressive tree due to its size and sturdiness, standing tall for many years. 2. This word also refers to a well-known and identifiable geographical location, a landmark in the landscape where people gather or pass by. In Judges 9:37, the oak of the diviners is a place that everyone recognizes, a visible signal on the path that descends from the country. 3. The oak could be associated with places of worship or religious practices, including divination. The oak of the diviners mentioned in this passage was likely a site where people came to consult or practice occult arts.
H0436G.origine: The Hebrew word אֵלוֹן (élon) literally means a large tree or an oak. It comes from a root that evokes strength and solidity. The oak was one of the most remarkable and durable trees in the Mediterranean region, hence its common use to denote a majestic tree or a landmark in the landscape.
H0436G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 9:37. In this passage, Gaal points out to Abimelech a people descending by the path of the "oak of the diviners." This is a geographical and tactical detail: a well-known tree that served as a landmark to locate troop movements. The context shows that the oak was a well-known gathering or passage place identifiable without ambiguity.
H0436G.portee: This passage reminds us that even in military and human strategies, divine Providence acts in the background. The oak of the diviners, a place of occult practices, disappears from the biblical scene: only the God of Israel truly guides events. For the believer, it is an invitation not to place trust in false oracles or divination, but in God alone.

sens: Large robust tree with deep roots and hard wood
Landmark in the landscape: place of passage, stop, or gathering
H0436H.detail:
1. The oak is a large tree well-known in the ancient Mediterranean, robust and imposing, that can live for a very long time. Its wood is hard and valuable, and its very deep roots make it stable. In Palestine, it is notably found in hilly regions. It is a tree that stands out in the landscape from afar.
2. For this reason, the oaks in the Bible are never isolated or anonymous: they are always named oaks ("oaks of Moreh," "oaks of Mamre") that mark a specific place in the territory. They serve as landmarks, stopping places, or gathering spots. Abraham dwells "among the oaks of Mamre" (Genesis 13:18), meaning he sets up his tent and altars there; it is there that God appears to him (Genesis 18:1). An oak can also mark a boundary or direction: "near the oaks of Moreh" serves to indicate where the mountains are on either side of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 11:30).
H0436H.origine: The Hebrew word אֵלוֹן (élon) designates the oak in a form that evokes strength and solidity. In Hebrew, it can also mean "plain" or "valley," a meaning that comes from the idea of an open space where these large trees stand. The oak is mentioned in several named regions of Canaan, suggesting that the tree was a major geographical marker for the ancient Hebrews.
H0436H.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular or to designate specific oaks identified by their location: the oaks of Moreh and the oaks of Mamre are the most frequent. Abraham dwells there and builds his altars, showing that these places are important for religious and domestic life. They are also landmarks for indicating directions or distances (Deuteronomy 11:30). A single oak is mentioned elsewhere: the oak of Tsaannaïm near Kedesh (Judges 4:11). The tree is never decorative or symbolic in these passages: it is always concrete, localized, a marker of territory and the presence of God.
H0436H.portee: The oak reminds us that the God of Abraham is a God who makes His presence known in concrete and named places, under trees where the patriarch sets up his tents and altars. These large, robust, and durable trees evoke the faithfulness and stability of the divine promise. For the Christian reader, they invite us to see God's Providence in the landmarks and places of our personal lives.

sens: Large robust and majestic tree, with hard and valuable wood
Wood from this tree, used for construction and objects
Tree in which or under which important or sacred events took place
H0437.detail:
1. The oak is a large tree characterized by its strength and solidity. It is an imposing tree that grows in the Mediterranean and Near Eastern regions, notably in Bashan (a fertile region east of the Jordan). The prophet Isaiah mentions it alongside the majestic cedars of Lebanon, highlighting its prestige (Isaiah 2:13).

2. The wood of the oak, hard and durable, was highly valued for the construction of ships, oars, and furniture. Ezekiel describes how the wood from Tyre partly came from the oaks of Bashan, used to make the oars and benches of the ship (Ezekiel 27:6). Oak wood was also used to make worship objects or statues (Isaiah 44:14).

3. The oaks marked the landscape of memorable places: it was under an oak, called the "oak of weeping," that Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, was buried (Genesis 35:8). These ancient trees became geographical and spiritual landmarks. They also served as places of worship, often idolatrous, where sacrifices were offered (Hosea 4:13).
H0437.origine: The Hebrew word אַלּוֹן (allon) specifically designates the oak, probably in contrast to other large trees like the terebinth. It is a word that describes both the tree itself and its practical value. In the Greek Old Testament, this word can correspond to several Greek terms depending on the context, as translators distinguished different species of oaks or robust trees according to the regions of origin of the text.
H0437.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, always to designate the tree itself. The usages vary: some passages refer to the oak as a tree of prestige and construction (Isaiah 44:14; Ezekiel 27:6), others as a tree marking a historical or sacred place (Genesis 35:8; Hosea 4:13). The prophets also use it in judgment speeches: Isaiah 6:13 compares the survival of a small remnant to that of the oak that sprouts again after being cut down, an image of resilience. The oak of Bashan is specifically mentioned for its superior quality (Ezekiel 27:6).
H0437.portee: The oak symbolizes in the Bible solidity, durability, and majesty. When Isaiah 6:13 compares the faithful remnant to the oak whose trunk remains after being cut down, it communicates hope: even in destruction, something essential persists. This word invites the reader to meditate on God's permanence through crises.

sens: City of the tribe of Naphtali in Canaan
Landmark serving as a geographical reference
H0438G.detail:
1. Allon is a city or place located within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali in the land of Canaan. Its name literally means "great tree" or "oak," suggesting that it was recognizable by a remarkable tree or an oak forest. In Joshua 19:33, Allon is mentioned as a boundary marker of the Naphtalite territory: "their boundary extended from Heleph, from Allon, by Zaanannim… to the Jordan." The name of the place helps the Israelites to precisely identify their territorial inheritance.
2. Beyond its geographical role in the division of the land, Allon serves as a stable and memorable reference point for future generations who needed to know the borders of each tribe.
H0438G.origine: The name Allon comes from the Hebrew root meaning "oak" or "great tree." Like many place names in Canaan, it originates from a natural feature or a visible landmark in the landscape. In the context of the territorial division of the Israelite tribes after the conquest, these names of trees or natural features served as easily recognizable and memorable boundary markers.
H0438G.emploi: Allon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:33. This verse is found in the section where Moses and Joshua list the precise borders assigned to each of the twelve tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. Allon marks a key point on the northern boundary of the territory of Naphtali, between Heleph to the west and the Jordan to the east. Its unique mention shows its importance as a memorable boundary marker rather than as a major urban center.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H0438H.detail: Allon is a man of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided. He is the father of Shiphi and the son of Jedajah (1 Chronicles 4:37). His name literally means "great oak" or "great tree," which was common for Hebrew names evoking strength and stability.
H0438H.origine: The name Allon comes from the Hebrew root designating the oak or the great tree, a symbol of strength and durability in biblical culture. This name, also borne by a city of Naphtali, reflects the importance of the tree in the landscape and imagination of the ancient Near East.
H0438H.emploi: Allon appears only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 4:37, where he is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon. He is presented as the father of Shiphi, who is himself the father of Ziza. This mention is part of the list of descendants of Shimeon, which reflects the importance of certain Simeonite families during the divided monarchy.

sens: The oak or great oak where Deborah was buried
H0439.detail: Allon-Bacuth literally means "the oak of weeping." It is a specific place mentioned in Genesis 35:8, where Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, was buried. The name of the place preserves the memory of mourning: they wept under this great oak for the death of this elderly and faithful woman who had accompanied Rebekah from her youth to her old age. This oak was located near Bethel, an important city in the land of Canaan.
H0439.origine: The name combines two Hebrew words: "allon" (the oak, this powerful and majestic tree) and "bakuth" (the weeping, the mourning). It is a toponym — a place name — formed to perpetuate the memory of a significant emotional event: the mourning of the inhabitants for Deborah.
H0439.emploi: Allon-Bacuth appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 35:8. It is the place where Jacob established a tomb for Deborah, the nurse of his mother Rebekah, when she died at an old age. Genesis also notes that she was named "Deborah" ("bee"), but it is her role as a faithful servant and her honorable burial that justify this memorial place.
H0439.portee: This brief passage reminds the reader of the value of faithful servants in the history of salvation. Deborah is not a heroine, but her presence alongside Rebekah for decades, and the honor Jacob pays her at her death, testify that God sees and values quiet dedication. The place named "oak of weeping" also shows how biblical faith honors memory and does not hide grief: we weep together for those who have served.

sens: Descendants of the clan of Elon, son of Zebulun
H0440.detail: 1. The Elonites are members of a family clan descended from Elon, son of Zebulun (himself a son of Jacob). They form one of the main lineages of the tribe of Zebulun and are listed during the census of the people in the wilderness (Numbers 26:26), alongside the clans of the Sardites (descended from Sered) and the Jahleelites (descended from Jahleel).
H0440.origine: The word "Elonites" (אֵלֹנִי) derives from the proper name Elon (אֵלוֹן, H0356), son of Zebulun. The Hebrew suffix -ִי (-i) transforms a personal name into an adjective or group name: it means "belonging to" or "descended from." The name Elon itself evokes either the idea of strength ("might") or a type of tree (the terebinth), symbolizing solidity and rootedness.
H0440.emploi: The Elonites appear only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:26, during the census of the second generation that came out of Egypt. They are mentioned among the descendants of the four sons of Zebulun, confirming their place in the structure of the twelve tribes of Israel. This census establishes the genealogical lineages before the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Close companion with whom one lives intimately
Domestic animal, tamed
Figuratively: long-time ally or confidant
H0441A.detail:
1. The word designates a person with whom one has a close and trusting relationship, someone one frequents regularly as an equal. In Psalms 55:14, the psalmist speaks of one whom he regarded as his "equal," his "confidant" — someone with whom he shared everything, even at the moment of betrayal. It is an intimate friend, not just an acquaintance.
2. The word can also refer to a domestic animal, particularly heifers or tamed livestock. In Psalms 144:14, the "fertile heifers" symbolize the prosperity and blessing of a nation at peace.
3. Figuratively, the word applies to one who has accompanied us for a long time, like an ally or a long-time supporter. Jeremiah 3:4 mentions the "friend of my youth" — the friend of olden days, the one whom one believed could be kept forever.
H0441A.origine: The word comes from a root that suggests the idea of familiarity and closeness: something or someone that has become familiar through habit and shared life. The basic image is that of a creature that has been tamed or domesticated, made docile through cohabitation — hence its connection with domestic animals. The meaning has extended to the human relationship of mutual trust, as a true friend is someone who has become familiar through intimacy.
H0441A.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Proverbs and Psalms, and in Jeremiah. It designates the trusted friend (Proverbs 2:17: the "friend" of youth who is abandoned), the one with whom the rupture is particularly painful (Psalms 55:14: the confidant who becomes a traitor). Proverbs shows how the friend is divided by quarrels and gossip (Proverbs 16:28; 17:9). Jeremiah uses it to speak of God as the "faithful friend" of the people, the one whom one should never abandon (Jeremiah 3:4). Everywhere, the word carries the emotional weight of violated intimacy or expected fidelity.
H0441A.portee: This word reminds the reader that true friendship — that which can be called confidential — creates a mutual obligation of fidelity. The betrayal of an intimate friend is a particularly grave crime, as shown by the psalmist's pain. It also invites contemplation of God as the faithful friend of our youth, the one we should never forget or forsake despite the twists and turns of our lives.

sens: Chief of a tribe or clan, who governs a group of families
Political or military leader who exercises authority
Powerful or influential figure in a region
H0441B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the chief of a tribe or clan — one who leads a group of families bound by blood. In Genesis 36, the "chiefs" are the sons of Esau and other ancestors, each at the head of his people: "These are the chiefs of the tribes descended from the sons of Esau" (Genesis 36:15). It is a familial and hereditary authority.
2. The word also applies to any political or military leader who governs and represents his people. When Moses recounts the flight of the Egyptians after the crossing of the Red Sea, he says that "the chiefs of Edom are terrified" (Exodus 15:15): these are the authorities who trembled at the news of God's miracles.
3. More broadly, it refers to a powerful or high-ranking man, a notable in a region. These chiefs enjoy a prestige and influence that give them weight in the affairs of their people.
H0441B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "mastery" or "governance." It is formed to designate one who leads, one who "holds the reins." The root is related to notions of authority and responsibility in the governance of a group.
H0441B.emploi: The word appears 60 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the genealogies of Esau (Genesis 36, repeated 20 times) and in 1 Chronicles 1. It is also used in later texts: in Zechariah (9:7 and 12:5-6), where it designates the military or political leaders of Judah and neighboring peoples. The context shows that it is an official title, recognized and hereditary, held by the notables of a tribe or nation. The word never designates a king in the strict sense, but rather a second-tier chief, a tribal or regional leader.
H0441B.portee: This word reminds us that God knows and mentions the authorities of all peoples — the chiefs of Edom as well as those of Judah. It also shows that true power does not come from the brute strength of earthly leaders, but from God alone: this is why the chiefs of Edom "are terrified" before His miracles. For the believer, this teaches humility in the face of worldly powers and trust in divine sovereignty.

sens: Campsite of the Israelites during the Exodus
H0442.detail: 1. Alush is a stop in the desert where the Israelites camped during their flight from Egypt. This campsite was located between Dophkah and Rephidim, along the route of the people through the Sinai desert (Numbers 33:13-14). It is one of the many places listed in the account of the journey to the Promised Land, where each stop was organized under God's guidance.
H0442.origine: The name Alush literally means "I will knead (bread)," evoking the idea of mixing or preparing. This name likely reflects a practical action related to survival in the desert — the preparation of food, a constant concern for the Israelites during their forty years of wandering. The name seems to have a descriptive meaning rather than a complex etymology.
H0442.emploi: Alush appears only twice in the Bible, both in Numbers 33, which lists all the stops of the Israelites' journey from the exodus from Egypt to the plains of Moab. This passage provides a complete and systematic itinerary of the camps. Alush is simply mentioned as a stop along the way, with no particular narrative attached to this place. The text only informs us that the people camped there before continuing to Rephidim.

sens: Gadite warrior who joined David
Korhite Levite
H0443G.detail: Elzabad is a man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. The name means "God has given" in Hebrew. According to 1 Chronicles 12:12, he was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who aligned himself with David, listed as the ninth among the officers who helped him. Another person bearing the same name was a Levite from the family of Korah.
H0443G.origine: The name Elzabad is composed of two Hebrew elements: El, meaning "God," and Zabad, meaning "to give" or "to grant." It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing the belief that God gives His gifts and blessings to His people.
H0443G.emploi: Elzabad appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:12. He is mentioned as one of the Gadite warriors who left Saul to join David at Ziklag, at a time when David was himself on the run. This list shows how powerful men rallied to David, recognizing that God had chosen him to be king. Another Elzabad, a Korhite Levite, is also cited in the genealogies of the Second Temple period, but with no additional details about his life.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Schemaiah
Warrior of the Korah clan during the divided monarchy
H0443H.detail: Elzabad is a proper name designating a man from the tribe of Levi, son of Schemaiah. He appears in 1 Chronicles 26:7 among the sons of Schemaiah listed as valiant men: Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad and his brothers, as well as Elihu and Shemaiah. This passage places him in the context of the Levites who served in the temple during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel.
H0443H.origine: The name Elzabad means "God has given" in Hebrew, formed from אֵל (El, "God") and זָבַד (zabad, "to give"). It expresses an act of thanksgiving to the Lord, celebrating the gift of this child as a divine blessing. This type of theophoric name was common in Israel.
H0443H.emploi: Elzabad appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:7. He is presented as one of the sons of Schemaiah, all described as valiant men (strong and courageous men). He is mentioned alongside his brothers Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elihu, and Shemaiah, in a list of Levites from the Korah clan. This mention suggests that Elzabad was a man of value and responsibility in the service of the temple.

sens: To become morally corrupt, stained in one's moral essence
To be tainted or vitiated in one's nature
H0444.detail:
1. The word describes someone who has become morally corrupt, that is, radically deviated from what he should be: it is a moral stain that affects the whole person. The image is that of a bad dye that permeates, transforming from within. In Job 15:16, Bildad depicts the man who drinks iniquity as perverted — deeply contaminated by evil, even in his essence.
2. The term applies to a state of alteration of moral consciousness: the person has lost his discernment of good and evil, he no longer does good. In Psalms 14:3 and 53:4, the psalmist asserts that all humans, without exception, are perverted — they have deviated from righteousness and have turned away from God.
H0444.origine: The Hebrew verb אָלַח (alach) fundamentally means "to corrupt" or "to be stained." It describes a progressive moral corruption, a spiritual decomposition. The term conveys an image of pollution or putrefaction applied to the moral and spiritual state of a person. It belongs to the family of Hebrew vocabulary expressing degeneration and alteration of what should be pure.
H0444.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the passive voice (Niphal form), and always in a context that denounces the moral corruption of humanity. In Job 15:16, it qualifies the sinful man as intrinsically perverted, stained by iniquity. In the two nearly identical occurrences in Psalms 14:3 and 53:4, the same verse affirms the universality of this perversion: all humans without exception are perverted and none does good. The word thus expresses total corruption, affecting the entire being in its relationship to God and to good.
H0444.portee: This word reminds the believer of the moral condition described by Scripture: without God's intervention, every human being is afflicted by a deep moral corruption that diverts him from good. It is an invitation to recognize one's own need for transformation and purification by God. It also establishes why only the Gospel, which offers a new birth and a restoration of moral consciousness, can address the fundamental problem of humanity.

sens: Israelite warrior during the united monarchy, son of Jaaré-Oreguim
Israelite warrior, son of Jair, who fought the Philistines
H0445G.detail: Elchanan appears twice in the Bible, in two closely related but distinct accounts. 1. In 2 Samuel 21:19, he is presented as the son of Jaaré-Oreguim, from Bethlehem, and the one who killed Goliath of Gath in single combat with a spear. 2. In 1 Chronicles 20:5, another Elchanan, son of Jair this time, is mentioned as having killed Goliath's brother, Lachmi of Gath, also in combat with a spear. These two passages show that under David's reign, Elchanan (or perhaps two men bearing this name) distinguished himself by his bravery in battle against the Philistines, the main enemy of Israel at that time.
H0445G.origine: The Hebrew name אֶלְחָנָן (Elchanan) literally means "God has been gracious" or "God has shown grace." It is composed of El (אֵל, God) and Chanan (חָנַן, to be gracious, to show mercy). It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing a divine blessing or grace received at birth.
H0445G.emploi: Elchanan is mentioned exactly twice in Scripture: once in 2 Samuel 21:19 and once in 1 Chronicles 20:5. Both occurrences present him as a warrior of the Davidic era who distinguished himself in fighting against the Philistines, Israel's major adversary. Both passages describe a single battle: one against Goliath himself, the other against his brother Lachmi. Both accounts mention a spear comparable to a weaver's beam, a characteristic detail of Philistine weapons in this cycle of warriors. The difference between the two versions (the name of the father and the adversary faced) has raised questions among commentators, but it likely indicates that there are two traditions or two different men.
H0445G.portee: The name Elchanan, meaning "God has been gracious," reminds us that strength in battle came from divine grace, not personal prowess. His role in the battle against the Philistines shows how God armed and granted victory to His faithful warriors to protect His people. These accounts encourage the reader to see, beneath the narratives of ancient warfare, the hidden action of God supporting His own in the face of their enemies.

sens: Warrior of Israel during the united monarchy
Son of Dodo, from Bethlehem
Military chief of David
H0445H.detail: Elchanan is a character from the time of David. He is a man of war, counted among the valiant leaders of the royal army. He is identified as the son of Dodo and from Bethlehem, the city of David himself (2 Samuel 23:24 and 1 Chronicles 11:26).
H0445H.origine: The name means "God has been gracious" in Hebrew. It is composed of two words: "El" (God) and "chanan" (grace, favor). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God and expresses a divine blessing.
H0445H.emploi: Elchanan appears only twice in the Bible, in the same passages: 2 Samuel 23:24 and 1 Chronicles 11:26. These two texts are part of lists of David's warriors, his "thirty valiant men" or his most illustrious military leaders. He is always listed alongside renowned warriors like Asahel, brother of Joab. His patronymic and local origin are consistently mentioned, suggesting he was a well-known and respected figure in the royal army.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Zebulun during the Exodus
Son of Helon
H0446G.detail:
1. Eliab is the designated chief or prince of the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the census of the people in the desert (Numbers 1:9). He represents his tribe during the organization of the camp and offerings (Numbers 7:24-29) and is among the leaders of the military divisions (Numbers 10:16).
2. He is identified as the son of Helon, which establishes his genealogy and status as a hereditary leader within his tribe.
H0446G.origine: The name literally means "my God is father" or "God is father," composed of "El" (God) and "ab" (father). This name expresses the belief that God is the protective and benevolent father of the people. The name reflects a common confession of faith in ancient Israel.
H0446G.emploi: Eliab appears only in the book of Numbers, always in accounts related to the organization of the people in the desert (census, camp, offerings of the Tabernacle). Aside from a namesake who is David's older brother and another who is a Levite musician, this specific Eliab is known only for his role as prince of Zebulun during the Exodus. The usages show that he actively participated in the cultic and military life of his tribe.

sens: Reubenite chief, father of Dathan and Abiram who rebelled against Moses
H0446H.detail: Eliab is a man from the clan of Reuben, living in the desert after the exodus from Egypt. He is the father of Dathan and Abiram, two men who participated in the famous rebellion against Moses and Aaron alongside Korah (Numbers 16:1). His sons rose up against Moses' leadership in the assembly and refused to respond to Moses' call (Numbers 16:12). This rebellion had terrible consequences: according to the biblical account, the earth opened and swallowed Dathan, Abiram, and their households (Deuteronomy 11:6), thus becoming a classic example of divine judgment on rebellion against the authority established by God.
H0446H.origine: The name Eliab literally means "my God is father" or "God is father." It is composed of the Hebrew word "El" (God) and "ab" (father). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the belief that the God of Israel is the providing and protecting father. Several other characters bear this same name in the Old Testament, each designating different individuals.
H0446H.emploi: Eliab is mentioned five times in the Bible, all occurrences found in the books of the Pentateuch: Numbers 16 and 26, as well as Deuteronomy 11. The first three references (Numbers 16:1, 16:12, and 26:8) identify him as the father of Dathan and Abiram. The last two (Numbers 26:9 and Deuteronomy 11:6) recall the context of his sons' rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and how God judged them by swallowing them into the earth. His name thus always appears in connection with this dramatic story of rebellion and divine punishment.
H0446H.portee: The story of Eliab and his sons illustrates the seriousness with which God takes issues of authority and obedience in His community. Although the Bible does not judge Eliab himself, his memory remains attached to one of the most serious rebellions of Israel in the desert, a warning for biblical readers about the consequences of contesting God's plan established by His servants.

sens: Eldest son of Jesse and older brother of David
Man from the tribe of Judah during the time of the united monarchy
Warrior who followed Saul
Ancestor from whom later generations descended
H0446I.detail: Eliab is the eldest son of Jesse, the father of David. He is presented as the firstborn of the family (1 Chronicles 2:13), which gave him a special position of honor. When the prophet Samuel came to anoint one of Jesse's sons to be king, he first turned to Eliab, impressed by his appearance, thinking that he must be the Lord's anointed (1 Samuel 16:6). Eliab accompanied Saul to war against the Philistines, alongside his brothers Abinadab and Shammah (1 Samuel 17:13). During the campaign against Goliath, Eliab expressed anger towards his younger brother David, who had come to bring supplies to the camp, accusing him of pride and malice (1 Samuel 17:28). This moment reveals the contrast between human judgment, which saw Eliab as the promising eldest, and God's choice, which preferred David's heart. Eliab had a son named Abichail, whose daughter became queen by marrying Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:18).
H0446I.origine: The name Eliab means "My God is father" or "God is father," composed of two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "Ab" (father). It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing the relationship of the bearer to God. Several other biblical characters bore this name: a son of Helon, chief of the tribe of Zebulun; a Reubenite, father of Dathan and Abiram; a Levite musician; and Gadite warriors. However, the Eliab in the provided contexts is clearly identified as the son of Jesse and brother of David.
H0446I.emploi: Eliab appears five times in the provided texts, all in the books of Samuel and Chronicles. He is first mentioned during David's anointing by Samuel, a key episode where human judgment opposes divine judgment: Samuel looks at Eliab's appearance and assumes he is the chosen one, but the Lord chooses David (1 Samuel 16:6). In the following passages, Eliab is presented as the eldest among Jesse's sons who went to war (1 Samuel 17:13 and 1 Chronicles 2:13). The most revealing episode is when Eliab reprimands David for coming to supply the troops, showing a fraternal animosity tinged with contempt (1 Samuel 17:28). Finally, it is learned that he is the ancestor of Mahalath, who became queen by marrying Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:18), thus ensuring a legacy for his lineage.

sens: Gadite chief who served David
H0446J.detail: 1. Eliab is a chief of war from Gad (that is, from the tribe of Gad) who joined David during his stay at Ziklag, before he became king of Israel. He appears in the list of mighty warriors who gathered around David (1 Chronicles 12:9), where he is mentioned as the third of the chiefs after Ezer and Abijah.
H0446J.origine: The name Eliab literally means "My God is father" or "God is father" in Hebrew, formed from "God" (El) and "father" (Ab). It is a typical theophoric name in the Israelite world, expressing a relationship of divine protection. The same name belonged to several other men in the Old Testament, including David's elder brother and other historical figures, but this passage from 1 Chronicles specifically concerns this Gadite military chief.
H0446J.emploi: Eliab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:9. He is presented as one of the chiefs of the Gadites who rally to David at Ziklag, before his ascension to the throne. This passage is part of a broader enumeration of warriors and chiefs who supported David during the period leading up to his official reign over all Israel. His rank as the third chief indicates that he held an important position of responsibility and military authority in his tribe.

sens: Levite musician serving in worship under David
H0446K.detail: Eliab is a Levite whose activity is mentioned three times in the accounts of the transfer of the ark to Jerusalem during David's reign (1 Chronicles 15-16). He is among the musicians chosen to accompany this solemn procession, playing the lute (a type of harp) or participating in the sacred orchestration led by Asaph. His name always appears alongside other Levite musicians like Zechariah, Jehiel, and Benajah, forming an instrumental ensemble in service of the presence of God.
H0446K.origine: The name Eliab means "My God is father" or "God is father" in Hebrew: it combines the word God (Eli) and the word father (Ab). It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a confession of faith by affirming the filial relationship of the bearer with God. This type of name was common in Israel to express piety and trust in divine providence.
H0446K.emploi: Eliab is mentioned three times in the account of the transfer of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem during David's time (1 Chronicles 15:18, 15:20, 16:5). In each occurrence, he appears among the Levite musicians selected to participate in this major worship ceremony. His instrument is specified: the lute (alamoth in 1 Chronicles 15:20), indicating that he had a particular responsibility in the musical accompaniment of the event. His constant association with Asaph, the chief of musicians, and with other instrumentalists suggests that he was a musician of quality and trust in the service of the house of the Lord.
H0446K.portee: Eliab represents the essential role of musicians in Israel's worship. The Bible honors his participation in the service of the Lord through his musical art, reminding us that music and art are gifts from God intended to celebrate His glory. His name itself — "God is father" — invites the believer to recognize in God a benevolent paternal relationship, especially in moments when we worship together, as the people of Israel did around the ark.

sens: Levite during the time of the united monarchy
son of Tohu and father of Jerocham
ancestor of the Korah clan
H0446L.detail:
1. Eliab is a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the people of Israel during the time of the united monarchy, that is, under the kings David and Solomon. He appears in the list of descendants of Levi passed down from generation to generation.
2. He is the son of Tohu and the father of Jerocham, which places him in a precise genealogical chain: it is known where he comes from and who continues after him. In 1 Chronicles 6:27, it reads "Eliab, his son; Jerocham, his son," clearly showing this father-to-son relationship.
3. Through this lineage, Eliab is part of the history of the Korah clan, an important group among the Levites. His name literally means "My God is father" or "God is father," a confession of faith integrated into his very identity.
H0446L.origine: The name Eliab is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Eli" (אֱלִי, my God) and "ab" (אָב, father). Its literal meaning is "My God is father" or "God is father," expressing the belief that God fulfills the role of father for the bearer of this name. This theophoric formation (which incorporates the name of God) was common among the Hebrews to affirm a personal relationship with God. Several Eliabs are named in the Bible: a chief of Zebulun in the wilderness, a Reubenite chief father of Dathan and Abiram, David's elder brother, and others; this one is specifically the Levite ancestor of Jerocham.
H0446L.emploi: Eliab is essentially a genealogical character in the Bible. He appears only once in the provided contexts, in 1 Chronicles 6:27, where he is listed among the ancestors of David concerning the musical charge of the temple (the group for which David was responsible). This genealogical list establishes the legitimacy and antiquity of the Levitical musicians of the temple. Although Eliab is an ancestor rather than an actor in reported events, his presence in this record shows that he was an established and recognized figure of the people of Israel during the time when the temple functioned regularly.

sens: A chief of clan from the tribe of Manasseh
Men bearing this name in the history of Israel
H0447G.detail: This name designates a chief of the Manassite family mentioned in the genealogies during the time of the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 5:24). The biblical text presents him among the "valiant men" and "chiefs of their fathers' houses," indicating that he was a man of power and influence in his tribe. Several other men bore this name at different times in the history of Israel — ancestors of the prophet Samuel, leaders in David's army, Levites — but only this Manassite is named in this verse.
H0447G.origine: The name Éliel literally means "My God is God" or "El is God" in Hebrew. It is composed of the divine name El (God) and the possessive pronoun "my" or "of me." It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the name of God, very common in Israel. It expresses the conviction that God alone is sovereign and trustworthy.
H0447G.emploi: Éliel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24, as one of the clan chiefs of Manasseh during the time of the divided monarchy. The biblical text mentions him among a list of six other "valiant men, renowned men, chiefs of their fathers' houses." This genealogical context indicates that the Bible preserved the memory of these important chiefs of Manasseh, even if the details of their exploits are not reported to us. Other men bearing the same name played a role in the history of Israel (notably under David), but this verse speaks only of this particular Manassite.
H0447G.portee: This name, borne by a man recognized as powerful and honorable, reminds us that God raises capable leaders among His people to guide and protect them. The mere fact that the Bible preserves the memory of this man shows that faithful acts, even forgotten by the world, are never forgotten by God.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H0447H.detail: 1. Éliel is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided. He is presented as the son of Shimei and brother to several other men (Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Élienai, Zilléthaï, Adaïa, Béraïa, and Shimrath), thus forming an important family in this tribe.
H0447H.origine: The name Éliel means "My God is God" or "El is God" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "Éli" (my God) and "El" (God), expressing a statement of faith in divinity. This type of theophoric name was common in Israel to express the religious conviction of the parents.
H0447H.emploi: Éliel appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 8:20, where he is listed among the descendants of Benjamin. The context of this passage is a genealogy of the families of the tribe of Benjamin during the period of the divided monarchy. It is possible that several men bearing the name Éliel lived at different times (ancestor of Samuel, chief in David's army, Levite, chiefs of Manasseh and Benjamin, chief Kehathite), but this one in particular is simply identified as a member of his family and tribe.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin
Military chief or notable during the time of the divided monarchy
H0447I.detail:
1. Éliel is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 8:22 as the son of Shashak. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, when the kingdom of Israel was split between the North and the South.
2. His name belongs to a lineage of chiefs and notables: several men bore the name Éliel, holding important positions in David's army, temple service, or the tribes. The context of 1 Chronicles 8 situates him in a genealogy of prominent figures.
H0447I.origine: The name Éliel means in Hebrew "My God is God" or "God is God": it is composed of "El" (God) and the possessive or an affirmative form. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing a confession of faith in the uniqueness and sovereignty of God. Several different characters bore this name in the history of Israel: an ancestor of Samuel, military leaders under David, Levites, and chiefs of the tribes.
H0447I.emploi: Éliel appears in 1 Chronicles 8:22 as a member of a genealogy of Benjaminites. He is classified among the chief or main families of Benjamin. Although the Bible recounts nothing of his personal life, his inclusion in this genealogical list indicates his importance in the tribal structure. Other namesakes bearing the same name held significant roles (warriors, Levites), but this passage specifically concerns the Benjaminite son of Shashak.

sens: Military chief in David's army
H0447J.detail: 1. Éliel is a military officer who served under King David. He appears in the list of David's elite soldiers, mentioned alongside other warriors like Jeribaï and Joschavia (1 Chronicles 11:46). His name and presence in this enumeration indicate that he held an important position in the military organization of the kingdom.
H0447J.origine: The name Éliel literally means "My God is God" or "God is God" in Hebrew. It is formed from the word Él (God) and the possessive pronoun or the repeated word for God, expressing a statement of faith in divine sovereignty. This theophoric name, which incorporates the divine name, was common in Israel and reflected the piety of the parents who gave it.
H0447J.emploi: Éliel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:46, where he is listed among David's warriors. The text places him in a list of military leaders who made up the royal army, particularly those who distinguished themselves in service to the king. His appearance in this role of warrior chief indicates his prestige and military authority under David's reign.

sens: Military chief in the service of King David
H0447K.detail: 1. Éliel is a military chief who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of warriors in David's army, in 1 Chronicles 11:47. His name means in Hebrew "My God is God" or "God is God" — a simple and direct statement of faith.
H0447K.origine: The name Éliel is composed of two parts in Hebrew: "Él" which means "God," and "i" which can indicate possession ("my"), or a simple affirmation. It is a theophoric name, meaning it bears the name of God. Several people bear this name in the Old Testament (an ancestor of Samuel, several Levite chiefs), but this text speaks only of this one.
H0447K.emploi: Éliel appears only once in the biblical texts that have come down to us: in 1 Chronicles 11:47, where he is listed among the valiant warriors who made up David's army. This list celebrates the men of valor who served the king of Israel. Éliel is cited there alongside other warrior names, without particular details about his exploits. This shows that he was well-known in his time to deserve this official mention, even though the Bible does not recount anything more about him.

sens: warrior during the divided monarchy, one of the leaders who joined David at Ziklag
H0447L.detail: 1. Éliel is a military leader who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. He appears in the list of mighty warriors who joined David at Ziklag, before David became king over all Israel (1 Chronicles 12:11). His name is listed among the first seven leaders, which indicates his high rank within this supporting army.
H0447L.origine: The Hebrew name Éliel (אֱלִיאֵל) literally means "My God is God" or "El is God," composed of the divine name El (God) repeated or intensified. This type of theophoric name, which incorporates the name of God, was common in Israel to express faith in the divinity. The root evokes divine power and the affirmation of the religious identity of the bearer of the name.
H0447L.emploi: Éliel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:11, where he is mentioned as one of the seven chief warriors who came to support David at Ziklag. This passage lists a series of mighty warriors who recognized David as their leader before his accession to the unified throne. The lack of additional details about his life or exact role suggests that what was important for the chronicler was primarily to confirm the military support that David enjoyed. Several other Éliel appear elsewhere in the Chronicles (ancestor of Samuel, Levites, tribal leaders), but the text does not allow us to assert that they are the same person.

sens: Levite who helped David transport the ark of the covenant
H0447M.detail: 1. Éliel is a Levite mentioned twice in the account of the transport of the ark of the covenant by King David. In 1 Chronicles 15:9, he is presented as the chief of the sons of Hebron, with eighty of his brothers under his authority. In 1 Chronicles 15:11, he is among the important Levites whom David summoned for this major ceremony. His name means "My God is God" — an affirmation of faith in the one Lord.
H0447M.origine: The name Éliel is composed of two Hebrew elements: El (God) and the possessive pronoun "i" (my), followed again by El, hence the meaning "My God is God." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing recognition of divine sovereignty. Several men bore this name during the monarchy, notably among the Levites and military leaders.
H0447M.emploi: Éliel is mentioned only in the First Book of Chronicles, in chapters 15:9 and 15:11, during the grand event of transporting the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem under the reign of King David. These two brief mentions place him among the most important Levitical leaders of that time. The context shows that Éliel held a major responsibility in organizing the worship and Israelite liturgy.

sens: A Levitical official during the reign of King Hezekiah
H0447N.detail: 1. Éliel is a Levite who lived during the time of King Hezekiah, around the 8th century B.C. He appears only once in the Bible, as a member of a team of officials responsible for the administration of offerings and gifts for the temple (2 Chronicles 31:13).
H0447N.origine: The name Éliel comes from Hebrew and means "my God is God" or "God is God": it is an affirmation of trust in the unique divinity of the Lord. This composition of the name reflects the faith of the parents who gave this name to their child, a common practice in Israel where names testified to the relationship with God.
H0447N.emploi: Éliel is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 31:13, where he is listed among ten Levite officials appointed to oversee the contributions destined for the temple under the reign of King Hezekiah. These men worked under the direction of Conaniah and Shimeah, and acted according to the orders of the king and Azariah, chief of the house of God. His name appears in an official list, indicating that he held a position of trust in the religious administration of the temple.

sens: ancestor of the prophet Samuel
warrior in the army of King David
Levite who helped transport the ark of the covenant
chief of the tribe of Manasseh
chief of the tribe of Benjamin
chief of the Kohathites
H0447O.detail: Éliel is a name borne by several characters in the history of Israel during the united monarchy and the early divided monarchy. The earliest is an ancestor of the prophet Samuel, mentioned in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6:34, where he is listed in the lineage of Levi; this Éliel is the father of Jeroham and the son of Toah. Other men of the same name served as warriors in the army of King David, as Levites during the transport of the ark, or as tribal leaders (Manasseh and Benjamin) and clan leaders of the Kohathites. These different Éliel were not the same person, but the name was honored among the Levites and officers of Israel.
H0447O.origine: The name Éliel means "my God is God" or "El is God" in Hebrew. It is composed of El (the divine name) and a verbal or possessive form. It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the name of God, a common practice in Israel to express the piety of parents and place the child under divine protection.
H0447O.emploi: Éliel appears several times in the books of Samuel and Chronicles. The given passage, 1 Chronicles 6:34, presents him as a link in the genealogical chain leading to the prophet Samuel himself. Other Éliel are named in 1 Chronicles as military leaders and Levitical officials under David and his successors. The name appears only once in the Segond 1910 (1 Chronicles 6:34), but the Bible mentions several men bearing this same name, indicating that it was a revered name in Levitical families and among the warriors of the kingdom.

sens: Son of Heman, Levitical musician during the divided monarchy
One of the choir leaders of the temple under the reign of David
H0448.detail: Éliatha is a musician from the tribe of Levi, son of the famous Heman. He appears in the list of temple musicians established by David for the service of worship (1 Chronicles 25:4). His name is also among those assigned a turn of service: Éliatha receives the twentieth lot in the drawing that organized the rotations of the Levitical musicians (1 Chronicles 25:27).
H0448.origine: The name Éliatha literally means "God has come" or "God has approached." It is composed of the element "El" (God) and a verbal form evoking divine coming or presence. This name expresses confidence in the active presence of God, consistent with the names of Heman's sons, all of which celebrate divine actions or qualities.
H0448.emploi: Éliatha is mentioned twice, both in chapter 25 of 1 Chronicles, which is dedicated to the organization of temple musicians under David. First in the general list of the fourteen sons of Heman (1 Chronicles 25:4), then during the distribution of duties: Éliatha receives the twentieth rank and is given twelve brothers under his authority to form his service team (1 Chronicles 25:27). These mentions show the importance of his role in the temple worship.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Benjamin at the time of the exodus from Egypt and the sojourn in the desert
H0449.detail: Élidad is a Benjamite chief mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the division of the conquered territory in the Promised Land. His role was to represent his tribe and ensure that Benjamin received its share of inheritance according to the plan established by God (Numbers 34:21).
H0449.origine: The name Élidad means "My God has loved." It comes from two Hebrew roots: "Eli" (my God) and "dad" (to love or beloved). This name expresses confidence in God's love for the bearer, a conviction characteristic of the great figures of the people of Israel.
H0449.emploi: Élidad appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:21, where he is presented as the son of Kislon and as chief of Benjamin tasked with participating in the drawing of the territory. His appearance in this official list places him among the twelve princes chosen by God to accomplish this crucial task: to transform the divine promise into territorial reality for each tribe. It is a role of honor and trust.

sens: Son of David, from the house of Judah, during the time of the united monarchy
H0450G.detail: Eliada is one of the many sons of David. He appears in the list of his children born in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:16 and 1 Chronicles 3:8). His name, which means 'God knows,' connects him to the other royal children of David. Although mentioned in the biblical genealogies, no particular event from his life is recounted in the sacred texts: he remains a historical figure of the Davidic lineage.
H0450G.origine: The name Eliada literally means 'God knows' or 'My God knows.' It is composed of two elements: the Hebrew word for 'God' (El) and the verb 'to know' (yadaʿ). This theophoric name structure, very common among the Hebrews, expresses a confession of faith: it is to entrust one's existence to divine knowledge. The same character is also called Beeliada in 1 Chronicles 14:7, a variant of the same name.
H0450G.emploi: Eliada is mentioned twice in the Bible: in 2 Samuel 5:16 and in 1 Chronicles 3:8, both in genealogical lists of David's sons born in Jerusalem. These two passages are variants of the same historical record. This is the only context in which this name appears in the biblical narratives — it is a character whose name alone has reached us, with no details about his role or actions. The mere fact that he is named among the sons of David shows his importance for the continuity of the royal house.

sens: Father of Rezon, an Aramean enemy of King Solomon
H0450H.detail: Eliada is an Aramean character mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Rezon, who fled from Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and whom God raised up as an adversary to trouble Solomon's reign (1 Kings 11:23). He is an example of the enemies that Solomon encountered at the end of his life, as indicated by the historical context of the beginning of the decline of his empire.
H0450H.origine: The name Eliada means 'God knows' in Hebrew, formed from 'El' (God) and 'yada' (to know, to be aware). This theophoric name expresses divine knowledge. Although Eliada is a non-Israelite, his name carries a religious formulation common in the ancient Near East. The name appears elsewhere in the Old Testament referring to other individuals (a son of David, a Benjaminite warrior chief), but this passage specifically targets the Aramean.
H0450H.emploi: Eliada appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 11:23, where he is identified as the father of Rezon. In this passage, the biblical author briefly mentions him to establish the identity of Rezon, the enemy that God will raise against Solomon. This mention fits into the narrative of adversaries that arise against Solomon at the end of his reign (1 Kings 11), marking the beginning of the decline of his political and military power after years of splendor. Rezon will later establish a small Aramean kingdom, demonstrating how Solomon's actions provoke lasting consequences.

sens: Benjaminite military chief during the Divided Monarchy
H0450I.detail: Eliada is a military leader from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King Jehoshaphat lists the commanders of his army. He is presented as a 'valiant man' leading two hundred thousand soldiers armed with bows and shields — one of the largest military units of the kingdom of Judah at that time (2 Chronicles 17:17).
H0450I.origine: The name Eliada literally means 'God knows' in Hebrew, composed of 'El' (God) and 'yada' (to know, to be aware). This name expresses the confidence that God knows all things and all hearts. Several individuals bear this name in the Old Testament, including a son of King David, but the provided text refers only to the Benjaminite chief.
H0450I.emploi: Eliada appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:17, in the list of military leaders of King Jehoshaphat. He is distinguished there as one of the most powerful officers of the Judean army, commanding the contingent from Benjamin. His name appears among other renowned leaders, highlighting his importance in the defense of the kingdom of Judah in the 9th century B.C.

sens: Fleshy and fatty part of the tail of the sheep or ram
Part of the sacrifice offered to God in Israelite worship
H0451.detail:
1. The fatty tail of the sheep or ram is the fleshy and fat-rich part located near the back, at the base of the tail. It is a highly valued part in the East as a luxury and flavorful food. It is mentioned in the sacrifices of Exodus 29:22 and Leviticus 3:9, where the text indicates that it is separated near the back.

2. In Israel's worship, the fatty tail is offered as a sacrifice consumed by fire before the Lord. It is part of the fatty portions that the priest must present as an offering to the Lord, along with the fat that covers the entrails and the kidneys. It is a regular element of thank offerings and consecration sacrifices, as seen in Leviticus 7:3 and 9:19.
H0451.origine: The Hebrew word alya literally means 'tail.' In the East, certain breeds of sheep develop a significant accumulation of fat at the base of the tail, which can weigh several kilograms. This part was considered a delicacy. In Israelite sacrifices, offering the fat was an act of respect towards God, as it was giving Him the best and richest of what one had.
H0451.emploi: The word appears five times in the laws of sacrifices, exclusively in Leviticus and Exodus. It always designates this specific part of the sheep or ram offered in sacrifice. In Exodus 29:22, it refers to a ram of consecration for the priests; in Leviticus 3:9, to the thank offering; in Leviticus 7:3 and 8:25, to the portions reserved for the priest in the sacrifices. The context is strictly liturgical and dietary: the word never designates anything other than this specific part of the animal, always within the framework of worship.
H0451.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that Israelite worship was not abstract: it involved real animals, precious meats, and a material respect towards God. Offering the best fat, the richest, meant giving what one had most precious, not out of mechanical obligation, but out of love. This illustrates the principle that true worship requires generosity and personal sacrifice.

sens: The great prophet of Israel during the time of King Ahab
Man clothed with the power of God to proclaim the word of the Lord
The one who calls the people to return to the God of Israel
H0452G.detail:
1. Elijah is the major prophet who intervenes during the reign of Ahab in Northern Israel, around the 9th century BC. His ministry is marked by spectacular miracles and a direct conflict with false gods: he stops the rain over the land (1 Kings 17:1), raises the widow's son (1 Kings 17:22-23), and confronts the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel by calling down fire from heaven (1 Kings 18:36-40).
2. Elijah acts as a man invested with divine authority to deliver the messages of the Lord. When he addresses King Ahab or military leaders, he speaks in the name of God: "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven" (2 Kings 1:10). His word does not return void — it accomplishes what it declares.
3. Elijah stands against the apostasy of Israel, particularly against the worship of Baal encouraged by Queen Jezebel. He calls the people to choose: "How long will you falter between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow Him" (1 Kings 18:21). His role is to turn hearts back to the true God.
H0452G.origine: The name means "My God is the Lord" or "The Lord is God" in Hebrew — elî (my God) + Yah (the Lord). It is a theophoric name, common in the Old Testament, which proclaims the fundamental conviction of the prophet: the Lord alone is God. The name expresses the spiritual identity of the prophet long before his actions. Several other people bear this name in the Bible, but Elijah the Tishbite of 1 Kings 17 remains the quintessential prophet to whom this name primarily refers.
H0452G.emploi: Elijah appears 62 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the books of Kings (1 and 2 Kings). His accounts span from 1 Kings 17 to 2 Kings 2, covering his calling, his ministry during the drought, his confrontation with the prophets of Baal, his sending against Ahab and Jezebel, and then his being taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire. He is also seen in 2 Chronicles 21:12 writing a letter to King Jehoram, and Malachi 4:5 announces his return before the day of the Lord. Each account shows him acting with supernatural power, speaking in the name of the Lord, and calling Israel to repentance.
H0452G.portee: Elijah embodies the faithful prophet who is not afraid to oppose religious and political corruption, even at the cost of his own life. His example teaches the reader that faith in the Lord alone brings victory, and that the true prophet speaks the truth without compromise. For the Christian, Elijah foreshadows the call to be a courageous witness for God in a hostile world. His being taken up to heaven without experiencing death also establishes the messianic expectation of a final intervention from God.

sens: Benjamite, son of Jeroham, brother of Shamsherai and others
H0452H.detail: 1. Elijah is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when it lists the descendants of this tribe. He was the son of Jeroham and had several brothers, including Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaaréschia, and Zicri (1 Chronicles 8:27). This is all we know about him: his name, his genealogy, and the fact that he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.
H0452H.origine: The name Elijah means "My God is Jehovah" or "Yah is God" — it is a theophoric name that associates a divine name (Elohim, "God," or Yah, a short form of the Name) with a statement of trust. This same name was borne by the great prophet during the time of King Ahab, very famous in the history of Israel, but the Benjamite of 1 Chronicles 8 is a different person, simply a namesake.
H0452H.emploi: Elijah is mentioned only once in the entire Bible: in 1 Chronicles 8:27, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Benjamin. He is among the descendants of Jerahmeel, listed without further detail. The context is purely genealogical — it consists of family records reconstructed after the exile.

sens: Priest of Israel at the time of the return from exile
H0452I.detail: 1. This name refers to a priest who lived at the time of the return from exile, when the Jewish people returned from Babylon. He is listed among the men who had married foreign women and who had to separate from them to remain faithful to the law of Moses (Ezra 10:21).
H0452I.origine: The name "Elijah" means "My God is Yahweh" or "Yah is God." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God to express the faith of the bearer. This same name was borne by the great prophet during the time of King Ahab, but here it refers to a simple priest of the return from exile.
H0452I.emploi: This priest is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Ezra 10:21. He appears in the list of priests and Levites who returned from captivity and who had to repudiate their foreign wives in order to preserve the purity of worship and faithfulness to God's covenant. His name indicates that his family professed faith in Yahweh despite the exile.

sens: Son of Elam who had married a foreign woman during the exile
H0452J.detail: 1. Elijah is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:26. He was the son of Elam and had married a foreign woman during the exile in Babylon. Upon the return from exile, the priest Ezra called upon the Israelites to abandon these mixed marriages to remain faithful to God's covenant: Elijah was among those who were invited to separate from their foreign wives.
H0452J.origine: The name Elijah means "my God is Yahweh" or "Yahweh is God" in Hebrew (אלי "my God" and יה "Yahweh"). It is the same name as that of the great prophet Elijah during the time of King Ahab, although this mention in Ezra 10:26 refers to a different man, living during the time of exile and return. The name was common in Israel as it expressed a confession of faith: recognizing that God alone is sovereign.
H0452J.emploi: Elijah is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Ezra 10:26, during the list of men who had contracted marriages with foreign women during the exile in Babylon. This context reveals a specific historical situation: upon the return from exile, the people of Israel sought to reconstitute themselves and reconnect with their faithfulness to God. Mixed marriages posed a threat to the religious identity of the people, and Ezra called for these separations to preserve the purity of the community. Elijah is one of the many names listed in this difficult passage, illustrating the moral and relational complexity of this period.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi during the time of the united monarchy, ancestor of Samuel
H0453G.detail: 1. Elihu is a Levite living during the time of the united monarchy in Israel, genealogically mentioned as the father of Jeroham and the grandfather of Elkanah. He is the ancestor of the prophet Samuel, according to the genealogy given in 1 Samuel 1:1, which traces back to Elihu among the ancestors of Elkanah.
H0453G.origine: The name Elihu means "He is my God" in Hebrew, combining the divine name and a statement of faith. It is a Levitical name that reflects the piety of the descendants of Levi, the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple.
H0453G.emploi: Elihu is mentioned only once in the provided biblical usages, in 1 Samuel 1:1, where he appears in the genealogy of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel. He is identified as the son of Tohu and the father of Jeroham, in the genealogical line that leads to the great prophet Samuel. His name also appears in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles under variations or parallel references.

sens: military leader of Manasseh who rallied to David
H0453H.detail: 1. Elihu is a Manassite war chief, meaning a military officer from the clan of Manasseh. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:20, where he is named among the warriors who left Ziklag to join David.
H0453H.origine: The Hebrew name אֱלִיהוּ (Elihu) literally means "He is my God" or "My God is he": it is composed of אֱלִי (eli, "my God") and הוּ (hu, "he"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the divine name and expresses a confession of faith in the God of Israel. This type of name was common in Israel to honor the divinity.
H0453H.emploi: Elihu appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 12:20. He is presented as a military chief of Manasseh who rallied to David during his establishment at Ziklag, before his accession to the throne. He is listed among other war officers from the same tribe, indicating that he held a position of military responsibility.

sens: son of Schemaiah, Korahite Levite gatekeeper during the divided monarchy
H0453I.detail: Elihu is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, son of Schemaiah. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. According to 1 Chronicles 26:7, he is one of the temple gatekeepers, valiant and courageous men tasked with guarding the doors of God's house alongside his brothers Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, and Schemaiah.
H0453I.origine: The name Elihu means "He is my God" in Hebrew: composed of "Eli" (my God) and "Hu" (he). It is a theophoric name, meaning it affirms a personal relationship with God. The same name is borne by several men in the Old Testament, including a young man who intervenes in the book of Job to rebuke Job and his three friends.
H0453I.emploi: Elihu appears only once in the Bible in the strict sense of this text: in 1 Chronicles 26:7, where he is mentioned as the son of Schemaiah and as one of the Levitical gatekeepers of the temple. He is part of a family of Korahite Levites, descendants of Korah, who were given the honorable charge by David to guard the doors of the house of the Lord. These men are described as "valiant," highlighting their physical strength and reliability in this sacred role.

sens: Son of Jesse and brother of David
H0453J.detail: 1. Elihu is a son of Jesse, the father of David, and a brother of the latter. He appears in the list of the twelve officers established by David to govern the tribes of Israel (1 Chronicles 27:18), where he is presented as responsible for the tribe of Judah — a position of honor and trust.
H0453J.origine: The name Elihu means "He is my God" in Hebrew. It is a compound of the elements *El* (God) and *hu* (he, third person pronoun), forming a statement of faith in the divinity. This type of theophoric name was common in David's family and reflected the piety of the ancestors.
H0453J.emploi: Elihu is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:18, where he is listed among the administrative officials of David's kingdom during the period of the united monarchy.
