This unique mention places him in the context of the governmental organization of the kingdom, revealing that David had given an important role to his brothers in the administration of the kingdom.

sens: young man who intervenes in the book of Job
son of Barakel of Buz
H0453K.detail: Elihu is a character in the book of Job, presented as a young man (Job 32:4, 32:6) who rises to speak after Job and his three friends have exhausted their arguments. He intervenes several times to defend God and criticize both Job and his companions, particularly Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar. His name means "He is my God," which summarizes his conviction: he believes that God is just and that Job is wrong to complain.
H0453K.origine: The name Elihu is composed of two Hebrew elements: "el" (God) and "hu" (he, meaning "my"), hence the translation "He is my God." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, like many Hebrew names in the Old Testament that affirm a conviction or a prayer of the parent who chose this name.
H0453K.emploi: Elihu appears exclusively in the book of Job (7 occurrences between Job 32:2 and Job 36:1). He is presented as "the son of Barakel of Buz, of the family of Ram" (Job 32:2). Unlike Job's three friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar) who listened to him for a long time, Elihu "had waited until this moment to speak" (Job 32:4) due to his young age. But seeing that no one finds an answer, "Elihu burned with anger" (Job 32:5) and launched into a series of speeches to reproach Job and his friends for their approach to the question of divine justice. After his four speeches, God himself intervenes (Job 38:1), but Elihu is never explicitly approved or disapproved by God.
H0453K.portee: The figure of Elihu invites the reader to reflect on the danger of arrogant youth and impatience in the face of God's mysteries. Although young and less experienced, Elihu dares to criticize both Job and his companions, showing how a certain theological assurance can blind us to our own limits of understanding. His example reminds us that there is wisdom in listening to those who have gone before us, even if we have new insights to share.

sens: Temple gatekeeper during the divided monarchy, son of Meshelemiah
H0454A.detail: Eljoenaï is a Korahite, meaning a member of the priestly tribe of the Levites, who served as a gatekeeper at the doors of the temple in Jerusalem. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of the sons of Meshelemiah enumerated in order of birth: "Elam the fifth, Johanan the sixth, Eljoenaï the seventh" (1 Chronicles 26:3). This role of gatekeeper was crucial in the functioning of worship: the gatekeepers controlled access to the temple, guarded the treasures, and maintained order during services. Eljoenaï held this important charge at the house of God during the division of the kingdom between Israel and Judah.
H0454A.origine: The name Eljoenaï literally means "toward Jehovah [are] my eyes" — a beautiful expression of trust and dependence on God, with eyes lifted toward Him. This meaning reveals what Hebrew parents desired for their child: a faith directed toward the Lord. The name carries the certainty that God is always the fixed point of the believer's gaze.
H0454A.emploi: Eljoenaï appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 26:3. He is the son of Meshelemiah (H4920), a Korahite from the family of the temple gatekeepers, and brother to six other gatekeepers: Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam, and Jehohanan. All these men served together at the gates of the temple in Jerusalem under the reign of David and his successors. This passage shows that temple service was a family responsibility among the Korahites, where the father and all his sons participated in this holy charge.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Descendant of David through his genealogy
H0454B.detail:
1. Eljoénaï is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms. His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of David (1 Chronicles 3:23), indicating that he was of high rank or at least that his lineage was considered worthy of mention.
2. He is the son of Neariah and the father of seven children: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelajah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani (1 Chronicles 3:24). These genealogies serve to maintain the continuity of the Davidic royal line even after the exile.
H0454B.origine: The name literally means "to the Eternal are my eyes" in Hebrew. This form reveals a prayer or a trust placed in God — the one who bears this name recognizes that his gaze and attention are turned toward the Lord. The name belongs to a family of theophoric names (containing the divine name) that were very common in Israel, expressing the believer's relationship with God.
H0454B.emploi: Eljoénaï appears twice in the Chronicles of Judah. He first appears as the son of Neariah in the lineage of David (1 Chronicles 3:23), then his name reappears in the following verse (3:24) to list his seven sons. This double mention indicates that his genealogical function was important to the sacred writer: it was about preserving the memory of the Davidic line through the period of political turmoil and exile.
H0454B.portee: Biblical genealogies like that of Eljoénaï remind us that God has never abandoned His people nor the promise He made to David. Even in the dark days of division and exile, the Lord watched over the descendants of the king. The name itself — "to the Eternal are my eyes" — invites everyone to place their trust in God rather than in earthly powers.

sens: man of the family of Pahath Moab who returned from exile with Ezra
H0454G.detail: 1. Eljoénaï is a man belonging to the family of Pahath Moab who participated in the return from exile under the leadership of Ezra, around the 5th century B.C. He is the son of Zerahiah and led two hundred men from his family (Ezra 8:4).
H0454G.origine: The name Eljoénaï comes from Hebrew and literally means "to Jehovah are my eyes": it expresses an attitude of trust and a gaze turned toward God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name (Yah, a short form of Jehovah), like many Hebrew names of that time.
H0454G.emploi: Eljoénaï appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:4. He is mentioned in the list of family leaders who returned from Babylon with the prophet Ezra to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. His main role in the biblical narrative is to testify to God's faithfulness in bringing His people back from exile.
H0454G.portee: The mention of Eljoénaï reminds us that the return from exile was not the affair of a single man, but of a multitude of families who chose to leave Babylon to return to Jerusalem. His name, which expresses eyes turned toward God, invites every believer to orient their life toward the Lord, especially in times of transition and spiritual rebuilding.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H0454H.detail: Eljoénaï is a man of the people of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were separated. His name means "to the Eternal are my eyes", which expresses an attitude of trust and expectation toward God. He is listed among a group of Simeonite leaders who multiplied and prospered under the reign of King Hezekiah.
H0454H.origine: The name Eljoénaï comes from Hebrew and literally means "to the Eternal are my eyes". It is composed of "El" (God) and "yoenay" ("my eyes toward"). This name reflects a vision turned toward God, expressing the expectation and trust of a person in His providence. Several men bear this name in biblical history, each in a different context.
H0454H.emploi: Eljoénaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:36, in a genealogy of the descendants of Simeon. He is listed among the military leaders and powerful men of his tribe who settled in Gedor and the surrounding regions. The context indicates that he lived during the reign of King Hezekiah, a period of prosperity and expansion for the people of Israel. This mention shows the importance of genealogies in the Bible for tracing the history of God's people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Beker
H0454I.detail: Eljoénaï is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Israel was in Egypt and in the desert. He is the son of Beker and the brother of several other men whose names are listed in 1 Chronicles 7:8. His name means "to Jehovah are my eyes", expressing a heart orientation toward the Lord.
H0454I.origine: The name Eljoénaï comes from Hebrew and literally means "to Jehovah are my eyes" (El = God, yoenai = my eyes directed toward). This composition reveals that the name expressed a vow or a conviction of the parents: the child was to have his gaze turned toward God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name and reflects the faith of the family.
H0454I.emploi: Eljoénaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:8, in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as one of the nine sons of Beker, alongside Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Omri, Jerimoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. This genealogical mention situates the man at the time when Israel was in Egypt and in the desert, but no specific event of his life is reported.

sens: Man living during the time of the Exile and the Return
Descendant of David
Simeonite
Benjamite, son of Becher
Priest at the time of Ezra
H0454J.detail: Eljoénaï is a proper name designating several different men in the Old Testament, all living during the period of the Exile in Babylon and the return to Jerusalem. The name appears mainly in connection with the return of the exiles. In Ezra 10:22, he is one of the members of the family of Pashhur who had to send away his foreign wife according to Ezra's orders: he is among the priests who had contracted mixed marriages contrary to the Law. The context indicates that he is a minor historical figure, but one that shows how the returning community was striving to purify and reorganize itself.
H0454J.origine: The name Eljoénaï literally means "to Jehovah are my eyes" — a confession of faith that expresses a gaze turned toward God. It is a theophoric name, composed of the word "El" (God) and a verbal form expressing orientation or attention. This type of name reflects the piety of the families of Israel and their trust in God, particularly relevant among the priests and the descendants of David.
H0454J.emploi: Eljoénaï appears only once in the Segond at Ezra 10:22, among the priests who had to separate from their foreign wives during the return from Exile. This passage shows that several men bore this name throughout Israel's history — descendant of David, Simeonite, Benjamite son of Becher, and several priests — but only this last Eljoénaï, priest from the family of Pashhur, is explicitly named in the preserved biblical texts. His appearance underscores the religious and social issues of the return from exile.
H0454J.portee: The name Eljoénaï, "to Jehovah are my eyes", reminds the reader that even the minor figures in the Bible bear names that express faith. His inclusion in the narrative of Ezra's reform shows that God takes into account each individual, every detail of the restoration of His people. It is an invitation to keep one's gaze fixed on God in times of correction and renewal.

sens: man of the time of Exile and Return
descendant of David
Simeonite
Benjamite, son of Becher
priest at the time of Ezra
H0454K.detail: Eljoénaï is a name borne by several men during the time of the Exile and Return in Judah. In Ezra 10:27, an Eljoénaï appears among the sons of Zatthu who had to send away their foreign wives after the return from Babylon. The name literally means 'to the Lord are my eyes' — a beautiful profession of faith, expressing that the one who bears it turns his gaze toward God. This name also appears in the genealogies of the tribe of Simeon and Benjamin, as well as among the priests at the time of Ezra, showing that it was quite common among the Jews who returned from captivity.
H0454K.origine: The name Eljoénaï (אֶלְיוֹעֵינַי) is composed of two elements: 'el' which means 'to' or 'God', and 'yo'enai' which comes from the root meaning 'eye' or 'eyes'. Together, it expresses the idea of directing one's gaze toward God, a vivid image of the attention and trust one places in Him. It is a typical theophoric name in Hebrew tradition, where the name expresses a personal relationship with the Lord.
H0454K.emploi: Eljoénaï is mentioned only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 10:27. He appears in the list of men who, upon returning from Babylon under Ezra, agreed to send away the foreign wives they had married, to preserve the religious and familial purity of the restored people. This historical context places him precisely at the end of the sixth century BCE, during the reconstruction of the Temple and the community reorganization after the Exile.

sens: Man of the time of the exile and return
Priest at the time of Ezra
H0454L.detail:
1. Eljoénaï is a man living at the time of the exile and the return of Israel from Babylon, a period when the Jewish people returned to rebuild the temple and the city of Jerusalem.
2. He is mentioned as one of the priests who participated in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, holding a trumpet to celebrate this major event (Nehemiah 12:41).
H0454L.origine: The name Eljoénaï literally means 'To the Lord are my eyes' or 'My gaze is toward the Lord': it expresses an orientation of the heart and soul toward God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes the divine name (the Lord). This type of name reflects the piety and hope of the one who bears it.
H0454L.emploi: Eljoénaï appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:41, during the account of the solemn dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. He is mentioned among other priests — Eliakim, Maaséja, Minjamin, and others — who carried trumpets for this ceremony. This context shows that he held an honorable priestly position and participated in the great religious celebrations of the restored people after the exile.
H0454L.portee: The name Eljoénaï, though little known, bears witness to the restoration of God's people after the exile and the continuity of the priestly worship. Its appearance during the dedication of the wall reminds us that even the less prominent members of God's people played a role in the spiritual and physical reconstruction of Jerusalem.

sens: One of the valiant warriors of King David
H0455.detail: Éliachba is a warrior mentioned in the list of 'mighty men' of David, those elite fighters who served him during the time of the united kingdom.
H0455.origine: His name, in Hebrew אֶלְיַחְבָּא, means 'God hides' or 'God is hidden', composed of אֵל (Elohim, God) and a root evoking the action of hiding. It was a common patronymic in Israel, borne by this man from Schaalbon, possibly a locality of the tribe of Benjamin.
H0455.emploi: Éliachba appears twice in Scripture, both times in the lists of David's elite warriors: in 2 Samuel 23:32 and in 1 Chronicles 11:33. Each time, he is identified as 'of Schaalbon' — a detail that distinguished him from other characters bearing this name. These lists, compiled during or shortly after David's reign, celebrate the men who contributed to establishing and consolidating the kingdom of Israel.

sens: Secretary at the court of King Solomon
H0456.detail: Elihoreph was one of the two secretaries of King Solomon, responsible for the administrative affairs of the royal court (1 Kings 4:3). He held a position of trust in the government, alongside his brother Ahijah, son of Shisha.
H0456.origine: The name Elihoreph means 'God of winter' or 'God of the harvest time'. He was the son of Seriah and the brother of Ahijah. This name, typically Hebrew, reflects the faith of the people of Israel in divine providence over the seasons and harvests.
H0456.emploi: Elihoreph is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:3, where he is listed among the high officials of King Solomon during the time of the United Kingdom. This passage enumerates the principal officers who ensured the administration of the prosperous kingdom under Solomon's reign. His title of secretary indicates that he was skilled in writing and managed official correspondence and court records.

sens: Statue or object made that is worshiped as a god
That which is vain, worthless, good for nothing
False word or prediction, false prophecy
H0457.detail:
1. An idol is a statue or object made by human hands — wood, stone, metal — that people worship as if it were a god. In Isaiah 2:8, the prophet describes the nations that 'bow down before the work of their hands, before what their fingers have made': this is the absurdity of idol worship, creating what one claims to adore.
2. The word can also mean 'nothingness' or 'worthless', which has no real value. When Job tells his friends, 'You are all worthless physicians' (Job 13:4), he is calling them useless and vain counselors: they talk a lot but heal nothing.
3. The term also designates a false prediction, a lying word from impure sources. In Isaiah 19:3, 'they will consult the idols and the enchanters': the word refers to the false prophecies that one hopes to hear from idols and diviners, baseless lies.
H0457.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of what is light, vain, without substance — something that has no weight, no solidity. An idol is therefore etymologically 'that which is worth nothing', 'that which is hollow'. The Hebrew word emphasizes less the external form that is worshiped than the nothingness it represents: a man-made object, incapable of acting, speaking, or saving. This is why the psalmist says of idols: 'They have mouths but do not speak' (Psalms 115:5).
H0457.emploi: This word appears eighteen times in the Old Testament, mostly among the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah). It primarily designates the statues of false gods that the nations worship — the idols of Egypt in Isaiah 19:1, those of the conquered kingdoms in Isaiah 10:10. In the Law, Leviticus 19:4 and 26:1 prohibit the Israelites from turning to idols. But the word also extends: in Job, it means 'worthless word' (13:4), and the psalmists use it to ridicule the impotence of false gods. In Isaiah and Ezekiel, God promises to destroy the idols, showing that despite the respect given to them, they are nothing but vanity.
H0457.portee: This word challenges the modern believer: idolatry is not just worship rendered to statues, it is also placing one's trust in what cannot save — money, success, self-image. Like the silent statues, these false gods can neither speak nor intervene. Scripture calls us to turn our gaze away from these vanities to the only living and true God. Recognizing that something is an idol is the first step to being freed from it.

sens: Husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Chilion
H0458.detail: Elimelech is a man from Bethlehem in Judah who, along with his wife Naomi and their two sons Mahlon and Chilion, emigrates to the land of Moab to escape famine (Ruth 1:2). He dies during their stay in Moab, leaving Naomi a widow with her two sons (Ruth 1:3). Although Elimelech himself disappears early from the narrative, his name and legacy remain significant: he establishes a family whose fields and rights of inheritance play a central role in the story of Boaz's redemption (Ruth 4:3, 4:9).
H0458.origine: The name Elimelech means "my God is king" in Hebrew. It is formed from three elements: "Eli" (my God), "me" (is), and "lech" (king). This theophoric name expresses a confession of faith: that the God of Israel reigns sovereignly. The name appears six times in the book of Ruth, always linked to family heritage and the question of land redemption.
H0458.emploi: Elimelech is a man from Ephrathah, a clan of Bethlehem in Judah, who lives before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy. The narrative of Ruth presents him as the head of a family who leaves his land to settle in Moab during a time of famine. His direct role ends at Ruth 1:3, but his name reappears constantly thereafter: it designates the original owner of the field that Naomi must sell and embodies the family line that Boaz commits to restore by marrying Ruth and redeeming the inheritance (Ruth 2:1, 2:3, 4:3, 4:9). Elimelech thus symbolizes family continuity and the order of succession according to the Israelite redemption law.
H0458.portee: The presence of Elimelech in the book of Ruth illustrates divine providence that acts even when faith seems to waver: a man leaves his land out of lack of trust, but God preserves his name and heritage for future blessing. His story reminds believers that God remains sovereign (as his name affirms) and that our misfortunes do not contradict His plan of salvation.

sens: Demonstrative adjective: refers to a thing or person present, visible, or currently in question
Reinforces the idea of proximity or current relevance of what is being discussed
H0459.detail:
1. This word is the Aramaic equivalent of "these" in French: it shows and designates something with a gesture of the hand or mind. In Daniel 2:44, "these kingdoms" refers to the four kingdoms just mentioned in the vision of the statues — it is a way of saying "the kingdoms in question, those specific ones being discussed." The word serves to draw the reader's attention to what is at the center of the conversation.
2. Sometimes, the word also carries the meaning of "render," as in Daniel 6:2 and 6:6, where the satraps "render" account to the king — but this is a usage specific to the Aramaic context, where the meaning "present" or "lead to" is close to the idea of designation.
H0459.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew אֵל (el, "this"). Aramaic and Hebrew are two closely related languages, spoken by the same people at different times. The word is a demonstrative adjective, meaning it shows and designates: it starts from the very concrete image of a finger pointing to something one wants to identify.
H0459.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Aramaic New Testament of the book of Daniel (2:40, 2:44, 6:2, 6:6, 7:17). It is used primarily when the text needs to remind the reader of what was being discussed: in Daniel 2:44, it refers to the four kingdoms of the vision; in Daniel 6:2 and 6:6, it designates the officials and satraps surrounding the king. It is a word of cohesion in the text: it connects what has just been said to what continues to be narrated. In the Segond, the translator has sometimes rendered it as "this," sometimes as "render" depending on the exact grammatical context.
H0459.portee: This word shows how the Aramaic Bible, like all texts, relies on small words to weave meaning. By reading Daniel attentively, one sees that each demonstrative creates a link between what has been seen (the visions) and what is understood (the future of the kingdoms). It is a reminder that God never speaks in vain: every word is tied to what we already know.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Gad during the census in the wilderness
Prince responsible for the order of march of his tribe
Son of Deuel
H0460G.detail:
1. Eliasaph is a military and administrative leader of the tribe of Gad, mentioned for the first time during the great census of the Israelites at the foot of Sinai (Numbers 1:14). He represents his tribe before Moses and the priest Eleazar during this organized count.
2. At each stage of the journey in the wilderness, Eliasaph leads his people according to the established order: he marches at the head of the column of Gad, guiding his warriors and families during the exodus (Numbers 10:20).
3. During the ceremonial offerings of the princes in the wilderness, Eliasaph solemnly brings the sacrifice of his tribe, signifying that Gad participates in the collective consecration of the tabernacle (Numbers 7:42-47).
H0460G.origine: The name Eliasaph means in Hebrew "God has added" (from Elohim "God" and the verb asaph "to add, increase"). It is a name of hope, expressing faith in divine blessing. According to some sources, Eliasaph would be the son of Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, which would connect him to a family of Midianites converted to faith in God.
H0460G.emploi: Eliasaph appears five times in the book of Numbers, always in contexts of administrative and religious organization of ancient Israel. He is mentioned during the census (Numbers 1:14, 2:14), during the offerings of the princes for the consecration of the tabernacle (Numbers 7:42, 7:47), and during the organization of the departure from Sinai (Numbers 10:20). His role is that of a tribal leader responsible for his people, ensuring their adherence to divine ordinances and their participation in collective religious life. He embodies the hierarchical structure of Israel in the wilderness.
H0460G.portee: The character of Eliasaph reminds us that God orders the life of the people with wisdom and that everyone has a place and responsibility in this plan: a leader must lead justly, organize carefully, and ensure that his community honors God. His very name, "God has added," expresses trust in divine providence during the trials of the wilderness.

sens: Leader of the Gershonites during the wilderness period
Son of Lael
H0460H.detail: Eliasaph is a Levitical leader who appears only once in the Bible, during the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness. He is designated as the head of the paternal house of the Gershonites (Numbers 3:24), a branch of the tribe of Levi responsible for transporting certain elements of the sanctuary — the wood of the tent, the cords, the veils — during the people's movements. His role was therefore to organize and lead this group of Levites according to the orders of Moses and Aaron.
H0460H.origine: His name means "God has added": it is composed of the word God (El) and the verb "to add" (yasaph). It is a name of thanksgiving, expressing the father's trust in divine blessing. Lael, his father, also bears a theophoric name ("God"), which shows that this family was rooted in the fear and honor of the Lord.
H0460H.emploi: Eliasaph appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 3:24. He is mentioned in the context of the census of the Levites that Moses and Aaron conducted to organize the service of the sanctuary and the transport of its equipment. His name is listed among the leaders of Levitical families, alongside other clan leaders (Elizaphan for the Kohathites, Eliasaph for the Gershonites, etc.). This brief mention reveals that God had established a precise and hierarchical order for the service of the temple, with designated leaders for each group.

sens: The Damascus servant of Abraham
H0461G.detail: 1. Éliézer was the servant of Abraham from Damascus. Since Abraham had no children at the time, he appointed him as the heir to all his possessions (Genesis 15:2). It was to Éliézer that Abraham later entrusted the crucial mission of finding a wife for his son Isaac, a task he accomplished with faithfulness and wisdom.
H0461G.origine: The name Éliézer means "God is my help" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: "El" (God) and "ezer" (help, assistance). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains an affirmation of faith in divine protection. The name reflects the trust placed in God for help and assistance.
H0461G.emploi: Éliézer primarily appears in the narrative of the Patriarch Abraham. Although mentioned explicitly only once in Genesis (15:2), he plays an important role in the story of Abraham's succession: Abraham designates him as a potential heir before the birth of Ishmael and Isaac. The name becomes emblematic of the faithful servant who carries out his master's wishes with dedication.
H0461G.portee: The story of Éliézer teaches Christians the importance of servant faithfulness and trust in God to guide our steps. It shows how God uses humble servants to accomplish His purposes and how faithfulness in small tasks prepares one for greater responsibilities.

sens: Son of Moses and Zipporah
Chief of a Levitical family whose descendants were numerous
H0461H.detail:
1. Éliézer is the second son of Moses and Zipporah. He received this name because, as Moses himself explains, "the God of my father has helped me, and He has delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh" (Exodus 18:4). His existence and place in Moses' genealogy are attested in the genealogical records of Chronicles.
2. Although Éliézer himself had only one son, Rechabia, this son had a very numerous descent (1 Chronicles 23:17). Through Rechabia, his children and grandchildren — including Isaiah, Joram, Zicri, and Shelomith — became heads of families among the Levites, thus attesting to his importance in the genealogy and organization of temple worship.
H0461H.origine: The name "Éliézer" means "God is help" or "God is assistance," composed of "El" (God) and a form of the verb "azer" (to help, to assist). This theophoric name testifies to divine deliverance. Moses chose this name to celebrate God's help against Pharaoh, thus marking in his son's name a memory of divine intervention.
H0461H.emploi: Éliézer appears four times in the provided biblical accounts, exclusively in the context of the genealogies of Moses and the Levitical families. He is first presented in Exodus 18:4 as the son born to Moses, already an adult when the Torah is given at Sinai. The other three occurrences are found in 1 Chronicles 23 and 26, where he is mentioned in the genealogical lists of the Levites organized for temple service under King David. His importance primarily lies in his descendants: although he himself had only one son, this son and his descendants held significant roles in liturgical service.
H0461H.portee: Éliézer embodies God's providence toward His people, his name itself being a cry of recognition for divine deliverance. His existence reminds us that children are a gift from God and a continuation of His salvific action. The numerous genealogy descending from him, although it passes through only one son, illustrates how God multiplies blessing and ensures the continuity of sacred service through generations.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of Egypt and the desert
Son of Becher and brother of several other Benjamites
H0461I.detail: Éliézer is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:8. He is listed among the sons of Becher, alongside his brothers Zemirah, Joash, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alameth. His name means "God is my help" in Hebrew.
H0461I.origine: The name Éliézer comes from two Hebrew words: "El" (God) and "ezer" (help, assistance). It expresses the trust that the father places in God to support and protect his son. This name was borne by several important figures in biblical history, including Abraham's servant and a son of Moses, but this one is simply a Benjamite whose genealogy is provided.
H0461I.emploi: Éliézer appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:8, where he is presented as a son of Becher in the genealogical list of the tribe of Benjamin. This passage enumerates the descendants of an important branch of this tribe, and Éliézer is included without further detail about his life or actions. His inclusion in this genealogical list shows the importance the biblical authors placed on preserving the memory of Israel's families, even for those whose personal history is not reported.

sens: Priest responsible for sounding the trumpet before the ark of the covenant
H0461J.detail: 1. Éliézer is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:24, where he is listed among the priests designated to sound trumpets before the ark of God during its transport to Jerusalem. He represents one of the priestly figures involved in this great religious ceremony during the time of King David.
H0461J.origine: The name Éliézer literally means "God is help" or "God helps" in Hebrew: it is composed of the divine name Eli (God) and the root azar (to help, to assist). It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing trust in divine assistance. Several characters bear this name in the Bible — notably Abraham's servant in Genesis 15:2, and a son of Moses in Exodus 18:4 — but this one specifically refers to the priest during the time of King David.
H0461J.emploi: Éliézer appears only once in the scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 15:24. He is named among a group of privileged priests responsible for sounding the trumpets during the solemn transport of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, a major event during King David's reign. This role indicates that he was a priest of rank and responsibility, worthy of participating in a ceremony of utmost importance.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
H0461K.detail: 1. Éliézer is a military or administrative chief of the tribe of Reuben, mentioned in the official register of tribal leaders established during the divided Israelite monarchy (1 Chronicles 27:16). He is the son of Zicri and represents his tribe alongside the other leaders of Israel.
H0461K.origine: The name Éliézer means "God is my help" or "God is my assistance" in Hebrew: it combines the divine name El and the verb azar (to help, to assist). This theophoric name expresses trust in divine help, a recurring theme in biblical names that confess dependence on God.
H0461K.emploi: Éliézer appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:16, where he is identified as the chief of the tribe of Reuben. The list he is part of enumerates the twelve tribal leaders responsible for administration and likely military defense under the monarchy. His brief but official mention indicates that he held a recognized position of responsibility in the political structure of Israel.

sens: prophet during the divided monarchy of Israel
H0461L.detail: Éliézer is a prophet mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is the son of Dodavah, from Mareshah. His name means "God is my help" in Hebrew. He appears in the account of 2 Chronicles 20:37, where he intervenes to criticize King Jehoshaphat for allying with Ahaziah, king of Israel, to build merchant ships destined for Tarshish. Éliézer prophesies that this alliance displeases God and announces that the Lord will destroy this work: the ships will be broken and will not be able to complete their journey. This is a classic prophetic act: the prophet speaks on behalf of God to remind the king of obedience and to show him the consequences of his choices.
H0461L.origine: The name Éliézer is composed of two elements: "Éli" (my God) and "Ézer" (help, assistance). It thus means "God is my help" or "God helps me." This name appears elsewhere in the Bible, notably for Abraham's servant from Damascus and for a son of Moses, but each occurrence refers to a different person. The name reflects a trust in divine help and was borne by several important figures in Israel's history.
H0461L.emploi: Éliézer, son of Dodavah, is a prophet who appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 20:37. He intervenes during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, probably in the 9th century B.C. His only recorded word is a prophetic judgment against King Jehoshaphat: he rebukes him for forming an alliance with Ahaziah for a maritime commercial project. The prophet announces that this association contradicts God's will and that the project will fail. This Éliézer illustrates the role of the prophet in the divided monarchy: to be the voice of God to correct kings when they stray from His commandments.
H0461L.portee: The testimony of Éliézer reminds Christians that God is concerned about our associations and projects, and that He can raise a prophetic voice to warn us. Jehoshaphat is praised elsewhere as a good king, but even he must give account when he makes choices contrary to God's will. The prophet does not hesitate to speak fearlessly to the powerful king: it is the boldness that comes from trust in God. Finally, this passage shows that obedience to God protects our endeavors, while alliances contrary to His will carry within them failure.

sens: Israeli leader during the exile and return
Name meaning 'God is my help'
H0461M.detail: 1. Éliézer is a Jewish leader called by Ezra to help him organize the return of the exiles to Jerusalem. His Hebrew name means "God is my help": a declaration of trust in divine protection. In Ezra 8:16, he is listed among the leaders that the chief of the return calls together to accomplish this crucial task: bringing the Israelites back to their land after the Babylonian captivity.
H0461M.origine: The name Éliézer is composed of two Hebrew words: "Éli" (God) and "ezer" (help, assistance). It is a classic theophoric name, which proclaims in its very form faith in divine help. Several biblical figures bore this name, including Abraham's servant in Genesis 15:2 and a son of Moses in Exodus 18:4; they all shared this same affirmation: their lives depended on God's help.
H0461M.emploi: Éliézer appears only once in the Bible in Ezra 8:16. He is presented as one of the leaders ("sariym") that the prophet Ezra gathers to successfully lead the return of the exiles from Babylon. His inclusion in this list shows that he was a man of responsibility and trust within the restored Jewish community, capable of participating in one of the most important undertakings in Israel's history after the exile.
H0461M.portee: The name of Éliézer reminds every reader that our leaders and authorities should not place their trust in themselves, but in God alone. Even in great and complex human tasks — here, the reconstruction of a ruined nation — it is divine help that remains the true foundation of success.

sens: priest who allied himself with a foreign woman during the return from exile
H0461N.detail: 1. Éliézer is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile in Judah. He is part of the sons of Joshua, son of the high priest Jehoiada, and he had married a foreign woman — which was considered a transgression of God's law at this critical time of the people's restoration.
H0461N.origine: The name Éliézer literally means "God is my help" or "God saves": it combines the word for God (Elohim) and the one that means "to help" or "to save." It was a name borne by several important figures in biblical history — notably Abraham's servant in Genesis 15:2 — but this priest from the time of exile is a distinct man.
H0461N.emploi: This Éliézer appears only once in the biblical records, in Ezra 10:18. He is listed among the priests and Levites who, upon returning from Babylonian exile, had married foreign women. The context shows that the religious leader Ezra undertook rigorous action to remedy these mixed unions, deemed incompatible with ritual purity and separation from idolatrous peoples. Éliézer thus represents a case among many others of this tension between integration and the religious identity of the restored people.
H0461N.portee: This humble character reminds us that even the servants of God and the priests of the chosen people are exposed to failures and compromises. His inclusion in the list of Ezra 10 shows us that the restoration of God's people after exile involved difficult corrections and severe decisions, necessary to maintain faithfulness to the covenant.

sens: man from the Exile and Return period mentioned in the book of Ezra
H0461O.detail: 1. Éliézer is a man who lived during the Exile and Return, that is, after the Jews had been deported to Babylon and then allowed to return. His name means "God is my help" in Hebrew. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:23, as one of the Levites who had to send away their foreign wives, in accordance with Ezra's orders to purify the returning community.
H0461O.origine: The name Éliézer comes from two Hebrew words: "El" which means God and "ezer" which means help or assistance. The name thus expresses trust in God as the source of help and protection. This name was borne by several important figures in Israel's history, including Abraham's servant, but the Levite in Ezra 10:23 is a distinct figure.
H0461O.emploi: Éliézer appears only once in the provided biblical references. In Ezra 10:23, he is counted among the Levites who married foreign women during the Exile. After the return from Babylon, the prophet Ezra organized an assembly to correct this situation, and Éliézer is named among those who had to send away their non-Israelite wives. This context shows that the Levites, despite their sacred status, had not escaped cultural and religious assimilation during the exile.

sens: Priest of Judah during the time of Exile and Return
One who separated from his foreign wife
H0461P.detail:
1. Éliézer is a priest belonging to the family of Harim, mentioned in the account of the restoration of the Jewish people after the exile in Babylon. He is one of those who took responsibility for ending marriages contracted with women from neighboring nations (Ezra 10:31).
2. This priest symbolizes the commitment of religious leaders to restore the purity and obedience of the people upon their return to Jerusalem, reinforcing the separation from the practices of pagan nations.
H0461P.origine: The name Éliézer means "God is help" or "God rescues": it combines the divine name Elohim (God) and the verbal root expressing help. This name reminds us that help and protection come from God. In the Old Testament, several men bear this name, including Abraham's servant and a son of Moses, but each person who bears it plays a distinct role in the history of God's people.
H0461P.emploi: Éliézer is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:31. He appears in the list of priests and family leaders who, under Ezra's leadership, separated from their foreign wives after the return from Exile. This action was part of the religious reform aimed at restoring fidelity to the law of Moses and maintaining the identity of God's people. His appearance in this context shows that the religious leaders had personal and moral examples to lead the community toward repentance.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H0462.detail: Éliénaï is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Shime-i and brother to several other Benjamites: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath. His name means "to God are my eyes turned," expressing an attitude of trust and supplication toward the Lord. He appears in the genealogy of the Benjamites established during the period of the Divided Monarchy (1 Chronicles 8:20).
H0462.origine: The name Éliénaï is composed of two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "ènaï" (my eyes). Literally, it means "to God are my eyes." This construction reflects a prayer or a profession of faith from the father who gave this name to his son, expressing his desire that the child keep his gaze turned toward the Lord and place all his trust in Him.
H0462.emploi: Éliénaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:20, within a detailed genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. This enumeration of Benjamite families was likely established after the exile or during the period of the Divided Monarchy, to preserve the memory of tribal lineages. His unique appearance in the genealogy shows the importance that ancient Israel placed on maintaining tribal and familial identity.

sens: father of Bathsheba
warrior of David from Gilead
H0463G.detail: 1. Éliam is the father of Bathsheba, the woman whom he saw from the roof of the palace and whom David coveted (2 Samuel 11:3). It is this Éliam whose daughter became queen of Israel and mother of Solomon. 2. Another man bearing the same name was a warrior in the service of King David and from Gilead, a region east of the Jordan. Although little known in Scripture, he is among the king's trusted men.
H0463G.origine: The Hebrew name Éliam literally means "God of the people" or "God is near," composed of "El" (God) and a term evoking people or kinship. In Chronicles, this same character is called Ammiel, an equivalent name that emphasizes this closeness of God to His own. This variation of name shows how ancient scribes could convey the same character under similar formulations.
H0463G.emploi: Éliam appears explicitly named only once in the text we are studying: in 2 Samuel 11:3, where he is identified as the father of Bathsheba. It is in the context of the famous passage where King David, seeing this woman from the height of his palace, becomes enamored and covets her as his wife. Although the name Éliam is mentioned only once in this verse, he plays a crucial role in the story as he establishes the lineage of Bathsheba and, by extension, that of Solomon. The genealogy of the kings of Israel thus passes through this previously discreet father.

sens: Father of Bathsheba, wife of King David
Warrior of David from Giloh
Son of the royal advisor Ahithophel
H0463H.detail: 1. Éliam is the father of Bathsheba, the woman that King David desires and marries after the death of her first husband Uriah (2 Samuel 23:34 mentions him in the list of David's warriors). 2. He is a warrior of David, a valiant fighter from Giloh who is among the thirty greatest warriors of the king (2 Samuel 23:34). 3. Éliam is the son of the royal advisor Ahithophel, an influential man at David's court, making him a man of high social standing in the united kingdom of Israel.
H0463H.origine: The name Éliam means "God of the people" or "God is my parent/ally," composed of the elements "Éli" (God) and "Am" (people or parent). It is a typical theophoric name of the time, expressing a relationship of closeness between the people and God.
H0463H.emploi: Éliam appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:34, in the midst of the list of David's elite warriors. He is presented as the son of Ahithophel from Giloh. His unique mention ties several important narratives of David's reign together: he is the father of Bathsheba, whose relationship with David will provoke a serious moral and political crisis, and the son of Ahithophel, who will later become David's rebellious advisor during Absalom's revolt.
H0463H.portee: The presence of Éliam in this list of faithful warriors, a few chapters after the account of his suicide following Absalom's rebellion, invites the reader to reflect on how David's sin has disintegrated the familial and political ties of his own circle. It reminds us that the actions of kings profoundly affect the families of their subjects.

sens: Eldest son of Esau and Ada, Edomite patriarch
Ancestor of Edomite clans through his seven sons
H0464G.detail:
1. Éliphaz is the eldest son of Esau and his wife Ada. He is born into the lineage of the patriarchs and holds an important place in the genealogy of Edom (Genesis 36:4, 10). As the firstborn of Esau, he inherits the status of chief of the elder branch of his family.

2. Éliphaz is the father of seven sons: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gaetham, Kenaz, Amalek, and Korah. These sons become the leaders of Edomite clans or tribes, meaning that Éliphaz is the ancestor of several peoples descended from Edom (Genesis 36:11-12, 15-16).
H0464G.origine: The name Éliphaz means "my God is (fine) gold." It is composed of two elements: Eli (God) and Phaz (gold, or perhaps wealth, fineness). The name thus evokes precious value and strength, qualities fitting for a prince of the house of Esau.
H0464G.emploi: Éliphaz is mentioned 8 times in the Bible, all in the genealogies of Edom: 6 times in Genesis 36 (the complete list of Esau's descendants) and 2 times in 1 Chronicles 1 (a parallel recap). These texts establish his descendants and show how the lineage of Edom is organized into tribal clans, with Éliphaz occupying the rank of chief.

sens: One of Job's three friends who came to console him in his misfortune
A man from Teman, a region known for its wisdom
H0464H.detail: Éliphaz is a friend of Job who comes to him with Bildad and Zophar when they learn of all the calamities that have befallen him (Job 2:11). He is referred to as "Éliphaz of Teman," a region reputed for its sages. In the book of Job, Éliphaz speaks several times to express his view of divine justice and the reasons for Job's suffering (Job 4:1; 15:1; 22:1), seeking to bring him back to what he believes to be the truth. However, at the end of the book, God rebukes Éliphaz and his companions for not speaking of Him rightly, unlike Job himself (Job 42:7-9).
H0464H.origine: The name Éliphaz means "my God is (fine) gold" in Hebrew, expressing a form of trust or affirmation in the divinity. It is a name that reflects piety, although the character in the book of Job reveals that formal piety can coexist with an imperfect understanding of God and His ways.
H0464H.emploi: Éliphaz appears six times in the book of Job, always in the context of the conversation between Job and his three friends. He is first introduced in Job 2:11 as coming to console Job; he then speaks three times (Job 4:1; 15:1; 22:1) to defend his theology that suffering is a consequence of sin. Finally, he reappears in Job 42:7-9 when God corrects the three friends for not speaking of Him rightly, and when they carry out what God commands after Job intercedes for them.
H0464H.portee: The story of Éliphaz teaches us that religious knowledge and sincerity of intention are not enough: it is possible to rigidly defend partial truths about God and miss His compassion and depth. Éliphaz illustrates the danger of judging too quickly the suffering of others and pretending to understand God's ways without humility. His example invites us to listen more and to guard against hasty certainties in the face of the mystery of human suffering.

sens: One of the valiant warriors of King David
H0465.detail: Éliphal is one of the most esteemed warriors of King David. He appears in the list of David's "thirty" or "mighty men," these elite warriors who supported him during his reign and battles. He is the son of Ur (1 Chronicles 11:35).
H0465.origine: The name Éliphal means "my God is supplication" or "my God is prayer," composed of "El" (God) and "palal" (to pray, to intercede). It is a name of faith confession that expresses the dependence of the bearer on prayer addressed to God.
H0465.emploi: Éliphal is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:35, where he is listed among David's renowned warriors. This list of David's "mighty men" includes those who participated in his victories and remained faithful to him. His unique mention shows that the Bible honors even those about whom little is known, as long as they have served God and His king valiantly.

sens: Levite musician in the service of King David
H0466.detail: Éliphelé is a Levite who served as a musician at the court of King David. He appears in the lists of musicians and gatekeepers of the temple during the transport of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18). He is mentioned again among those who played the eight-stringed harp to lead the singing in worship (1 Chronicles 15:21). His role was thus to animate the temple liturgy through his music, alongside other Levite musicians like Obed-Edom and Jeiel.
H0466.origine: The name Éliphelé means "my God has set apart" or "my God distinguishes." It is a theophoric Hebrew name composed of the word "Eli" (my God) and the root "phlh" (to set apart, to distinguish). The name expresses the conviction that this man had been chosen and separated by God for a particular mission in the service of the temple.
H0466.emploi: Éliphelé is a minor character from the time of the divided monarchy, mentioned only twice in 1 Chronicles 15. Both references place him in the context of the solemn procession of the Ark of the Covenant organized by King David. In 1 Chronicles 15:18, he is listed among the musicians for this occasion, while in 1 Chronicles 15:21, he is specifically identified as one of those who played the eight-stringed harp to lead the liturgical singing. These two mentions show that Éliphelé was a recognized and respected musician in ancient Israelite worship.
H0466.portee: Éliphelé illustrates the important role that the Bible assigns to music in the public worship of the temple. His inclusion in the lists of temple servants reminds us that serving God was a collective affair, entrusted to men dedicated to various tasks — here, enriching worship through music. For the Christian reader, this figure encourages us to view church music not as entertainment, but as a true form of service rendered to the Lord.

sens: Son of David, king of Israel
One of David's mighty warriors
Benjaminite descendant of Jonathan
Clan leader among the descendants of Adonikam
Member of the lineage of Hashum
H0467G.detail:
1. Éliphéleth is one of the sons of David born in Jerusalem, mentioned in the lists of the king's children (2 Samuel 5:16; 1 Chronicles 3:8). He is among the many sons that David had with several women during his reign in Jerusalem.

2. Another Éliphéleth appears as one of David's warriors — elite soldiers who followed and fought alongside him.

3. A Benjaminite Éliphéleth is mentioned as a descendant of King Saul through the line of Jonathan, showing that there were other people bearing this famous name among the people of Israel.

4. An Éliphéleth also appears as a leader of a family or clan, notably among the descendants of Adonikam, and as a member of the line of Hashum — family names that participated in the return from exile.
H0467G.origine: The name Éliphéleth (אֲלִיפֶלֶט in Hebrew) literally means "God is deliverance": it combines "El" (God) and a word evoking deliverance or escape. It is a theophoric name — that is, it bears the divine name — formed to express that God is the one who saves and protects. This type of name was common in the Davidic royal family, expressing the hope placed in God.
H0467G.emploi: Éliphéleth designates at least five different characters in the Bible, all bearing this same prestigious name. The most well-known is the son of David mentioned three times in Scripture (2 Samuel 5:16; 1 Chronicles 3:8 and 14:7): he appears in the official lists of the king's children born in Jerusalem, confirming his status as a direct member of the royal family. Other Éliphéleth appear in the history of Israel (warriors, descendants of Jonathan, clan leaders), but the provided biblical references concern only the son of David.
H0467G.portee: This name reminds the reader of a central truth of faith: God is deliverance. For the ancient Israelites who heard this name in the royal family, it was an affirmation that the Lord protected the king and his descendants. Even for us today, this name evokes that our trust and hope must rest in God alone, who remains our deliverer in the face of peril and adversity.

sens: A warrior among David's mighty men
H0467H.detail: 1. Éliphéleth is a warrior who fought alongside King David, counting among his "mighty men" (2 Samuel 23:34). He appears in the list of the most renowned warriors of the kingdom, which shows his role as a respected fighter.
H0467H.origine: The name Éliphéleth means "God is deliverance" (in Hebrew: Éli = God, and péleth = deliverance or salvation). This composition reflects a trust in divine protection, typical of the theophoric names of the Israelite monarchy period.
H0467H.emploi: Éliphéleth appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:34, where he is mentioned as the son of Ahasbai (a Maacathite) and counts among the 30 elite warriors of King David. This list celebrates the bravest men of David's reign, and Éliphéleth occupies an honorable place in it, indicating his military importance and prestige at the royal court.

sens: Son of David and Bathsheba, mentioned among the children born in Jerusalem
Young son of David, brother of Solomon
H0467I.detail: 1. Éliphéleth is one of the sons of David, born from his union with Bathsheba in Jerusalem. He appears in the genealogical lists of the united monarchy of Israel, placed among the officially recognized children of the king.
H0467I.origine: The name means "God is deliverance" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: "El" (God) and "pelet" (deliverance, escape). It is a theophoric name, common in the royal family of Judah, expressing trust in divine protection.
H0467I.emploi: Éliphéleth appears in two parallel passages in Chronicles, which enumerate the sons of David born in Jerusalem. These genealogical lists from David's reign show that several of his sons bore names expressing divine providence. He was likely a young child at the time these lists were compiled, as he is never mentioned in historical accounts as having played a political or military role at court.

sens: Descendant of Benjamin and Elah, living during the divided monarchy
Son of Eshech and brother of Ulam and Jeush
H0467J.detail: Éliphéleth is a member of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the genealogies of the Bible. He appears as the third son of Eshech (1 Chronicles 8:39), himself a descendant of Jonathan, the son of King Saul. His name means "God is deliverance," reflecting the trust of God's people in divine protection.
H0467J.origine: The name Éliphéleth comes from two Hebrew elements: "Eli" (God) and "pelet" (deliverance). It is a typical theophoric name in Israel that expresses the conviction that only God can save and deliver His people. Several biblical characters bear this name or similar variants, showing its importance in Israelite onomastics.
H0467J.emploi: Éliphéleth is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 8:39, where he is presented as the third son of Eshech in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. This passage is part of the long list of descendants of Benjamin and Jonathan, son of King Saul. Although little known, Éliphéleth fits into the genealogical continuity of the people of Israel and its nobility. He lived during the period of the divided monarchy.

sens: Chief of a family who returned from exile to Jerusalem
H0467K.detail: Éliphéleth is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return of the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem. He is presented as one of the family heads of the Adonikam clan, responsible for his relatives who returned with Ezra. His name means "God is deliverance" or "God is my salvation," reflecting the hope of the exiles who found the possibility to return to their land.
H0467K.origine: The name Éliphéleth comes from Hebrew and is composed of two elements: "El" (God) and a root that evokes deliverance or salvation. This name belongs to a family of compound names with "God" that are very common in the Old Testament. Several people bore this name at different times in Israel's history: sons of David, warriors, and members of the people who returned from exile.
H0467K.emploi: Éliphéleth appears in Ezra 8:13 as one of the three heads of the Adonikam family who accompany Ezra during the return of the exiles, around 458 B.C. He is responsible for sixty men of his family. His appearance in this list from Ezra shows that he held an important role in the organization of the return and the reconstruction of the Jewish community in Jerusalem.

sens: Man from the line of Hashum, mentioned during the exile and return
H0467L.detail: 1. Éliphéleth is a proper name designating a man from the genealogy of Hashum, an important family in Israel. He appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:33, among those who had married foreign women and had to separate from them upon returning from exile.
H0467L.origine: The name Éliphéleth means "God is deliverance" in Hebrew, composed of El ("God") and pelet ("deliverance"). This name appears several times in the Old Testament to designate different people: notably a son of David, warriors from his court, and descendants of Benjamin. In this specific case, he is a member of the Hashum family.
H0467L.emploi: Éliphéleth appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:33. This passage recounts the moment when, after the return from exile to Jerusalem, Ezra and the leaders of the people discovered that some Israelites had married women from neighboring peoples, contrary to the Law. Éliphéleth is among those from the house of Hashum who had to send away their foreign wives. This name reminds us of how the restored community of God's people had to purify and reorganize itself.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Reuben during the Exodus and the wilderness period
Son of Shedeur
Prince responsible for the order and organization of the camp of Reuben
H0468.detail: Élitsur is a military and administrative leader of the tribe of Reuben during the years in the desert. His name means "my God is a rock" or "the rock is God," expressing that God is the solid and unshakeable foundation upon which the people can rely. He appears as prince (chief) of his tribe, responsible for placing the camp of Reuben in the order prescribed by God, and leading his contingent during the marches (Numbers 1:5; Numbers 2:10). He also offers the thank offerings on behalf of his tribe, detailed during the dedication of the Tabernacle (Numbers 7:30-35). He is a trustworthy man to whom God entrusts the charge of representing and guiding his tribe.
H0468.origine: The Hebrew name אֱלִיצוּר is composed of two elements: אֱלִי (eli, "my God") and צוּר (tsur, "rock"). The word "rock" in the Bible evokes solidity, protection, and certainty — God is often called the rock upon which one relies. This name reflects the faith confession of Élitsur's parents: God alone is the stable and reliable foundation of the people.
H0468.emploi: Élitsur is mentioned five times in the book of Numbers, always in relation to the census and organization of the people in the desert. He first appears during the counting of the Israelites at the foot of Sinai, where he is designated as prince of Reuben (Numbers 1:5). He is then found in the camping instructions, where he is given the responsibility to position the banner and the army of Reuben to the south of the camp (Numbers 2:10). During the dedication of the Tabernacle, he is among the leaders who offer the thank offerings (Numbers 7:30-35). Finally, at the beginning of the march from Sinai, he leads the military deployment of his tribe (Numbers 10:18). His role remains constant: a responsible and trustworthy leader.
H0468.portee: Élitsur embodies the importance of servant leadership in God's people. His name proclaims that God alone is the rock, the foundation — not the leader himself. This reminds the believer that every leader, every guide, must recognize that God is the source of strength, order, and blessing. Élitsur's faithfulness in carrying out divine directives, from the census to the sacrifices and the marches, shows how a servant of the Lord should operate: in concrete obedience and order, knowing that God is the true Leader.

sens: Son of Uzziel and brother of Mishael, a Levite from the family of Kohath during the time of Moses
Chief of the Kohathite clan in the desert
Levite who helped remove the bodies of Abihu and Nadab after their death
H0469G.detail:
1. Élitsaphan is a member of the tribe of Levi, belonging to the family of the Kohathites. He is the son of Uzziel and the brother of Mishael, Sithri, and Micah (Exodus 6:22). His name means "my God has protected."

2. He is designated as the chief of the paternal house of the families of the Kohathites (Numbers 3:30), responsible for leading this important group within the Levites.

3. When the sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, die by the fire of the Lord, Moses calls upon Élitsaphan and Mishael to remove the bodies of their brothers and take them outside the sanctuary (Leviticus 10:4). This is a serious task entrusted to this trustworthy man.
H0469G.origine: The Hebrew name אֱלִיצָפָן (Élitsaphan) is composed of אֱלִי (Eli, "my God") and צָפַן (tsaphan, "to protect" or "to hide safely"). It expresses faith in divine protection. This name also appears in the form Eltsaphan in biblical texts (Exodus 6:22), both forms being acceptable in Hebrew.
H0469G.emploi: Élitsaphan appears in five biblical passages, all dating from the time of Moses and the early monarchy. He is first identified as the son of Uzziel in Exodus 6:22, at the time of the genealogy of the Levites. In Leviticus 10:4, he receives a delicate mission: to remove the bodies of Nadab and Abihu. In Numbers 3:30, he is officially named chief of the Kohathites, which shows his importance in the organization of the people. Two later references (1 Chronicles 15:8 and 2 Chronicles 29:13) mention his descendants, expanding his lineage and influence through generations in the Levitical ministry.
H0469G.portee: Élitsaphan embodies the trustworthy man called by God for serious responsibilities. His name reminds us that divine protection accompanies those who faithfully serve the Lord. His story shows how God relies on men and families dedicated to sacred service, and how these responsibilities are passed down through subsequent generations.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Zebulun
Son of Parnach
H0469H.detail:
1. Élitsaphan is a prince (chief) designated to represent the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the promised land (Numbers 34:25). He belongs to a generation that crossed the desert and receives an important administrative responsibility in the organization of the territory.
2. He is the son of Parnach, indicating his genealogy and hereditary status within his tribe.
H0469H.origine: The name Élitsaphan means "my God has protected" in Hebrew. It comes from the root meaning "to protect" or "to keep," thus expressing the belief that the Lord was the protector of this chief and his lineage. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) is common among the Israelites.
H0469H.emploi: Élitsaphan appears only once in Scripture, in Numbers 34:25. Moses establishes responsible men to oversee the division of the territory of Canaan among the tribes of Israel. Élitsaphan is named as the prince representing Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes. His appearance in this context underscores the administrative importance and order that God establishes for the organization of the people in the promised land.

sens: One of the valiant warriors of King David
H0470.detail: Élika is a warrior who served under the command of King David, listed among the "mighty men" whose memory is preserved in the Bible (2 Samuel 23:25). He came from the city of Harod. This is the only place where the Bible mentions him.
H0470.origine: His name means "my God rejects" in Hebrew, formed from the verb meaning "to reject" preceded by the possessive "my." It is a theophoric name, that is, a name that contains a reference to God, quite common in ancient Israel.
H0470.emploi: Élika appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:25, in the list of David's thirty elite warriors. This list enumerates the most courageous and loyal men of the king, those who fought by his side. Élika is simply mentioned with his city of origin, Harod, without detail about his particular exploits.

sens: Son of Hilkiah, chief of the king Hezekiah's house during the Assyrian invasion
Son of Josiah, enthroned by Pharaoh Necho under the name of Jehoiakim
Priest who assisted Nehemiah at the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem
H0471G.detail: 1. Éliakim, son of Hilkiah, was the principal minister of Hezekiah at the time of the invasion of the kingdom of Judah by Assyria. He directed the royal house (2 Kings 18:18) and represented the king in the most serious negotiations, notably with the Assyrian general Rabshakeh and the prophet Isaiah. 2. Another Éliakim, son of King Josiah, was placed on the throne of Judah by Pharaoh Necho after the death of his father, and renamed Jehoiakim. 3. A third Éliakim is mentioned among the priests who participated in the ceremony of dedication of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah.
H0471G.origine: The name Éliakim means "God raises" or "God establishes," composed of El (God) and a form of the verb meaning "to rise" or "to establish." This name expresses the certainty that God supports and lifts up the one who bears it.
H0471G.emploi: The name Éliakim appears nine times in the Bible, primarily in the context of Hezekiah's reign. Éliakim son of Hilkiah is mentioned six times in 2 Kings 18-19 and Isaiah 36-37: he accompanies the king in this major crisis where Judah faces the Assyrian threat, speaking with the Assyrian chief and reporting his words to the king and the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 22:20 contains a remarkable prophetic word where God promises to call Éliakim as his servant, evoking a role of stability and trust. The remaining references pertain to Éliakim son of Josiah and the priest during Nehemiah's time.
H0471G.portee: Éliakim represents the faithful servant of God in a position of power and responsibility, particularly in times of crisis. His example shows how one who holds an important office must serve his king with integrity, seek counsel from the prophets, and depend on God rather than his own strength.

sens: Priest who participated in the dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time
H0471H.detail: 1. Éliakim is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the great dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem, just after the return from exile. He is among the priests who formed a festive procession with trumpets to celebrate this important moment of the reconstruction of the temple and the Jewish community (Nehemiah 12:41).
H0471H.origine: The name Éliakim literally means "God raises" or "God establishes" in Hebrew, formed from El (God) and the verb qoum (to rise, to establish). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing confidence in God's saving action. Although the name has designated other characters in Israel's history — notably a son of King Josiah and a minister of King Hezekiah — only this priest from Nehemiah's time is mentioned in this passage.
H0471H.emploi: Éliakim appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:41, during the description of the procession of priests and Levites for the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. He is named among other priests, all bearing trumpets, indicating that he held a role of responsibility in the worship of the restored temple. This moment marked the end of the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the establishment of worship in the second temple.

sens: Son of Josiah, king of Judah appointed by the Egyptian Pharaoh Necho
Name also borne by the master of the palace of King Hezekiah and by a priest during the time of Nehemiah
H0471I.detail: 1. Eliakim is the son of King Josiah of Judah. After his father's death, Pharaoh Necho of Egypt places him on the throne in place of his brother Jehoahaz, and changes his name to Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:34 and 2 Chronicles 36:4). This name change marked Judah's subjugation to Egypt. 2. The same name is borne by other lesser-known biblical figures: a steward of the palace of King Hezekiah, and a priest who assisted Nehemiah in the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile.
H0471I.origine: The name Eliakim means "God raises" or "God establishes": it is formed from two Hebrew words, El (God) and yakim (he raises, he establishes). This name expresses a trust in divine power to uplift and strengthen. Several biblical characters have borne this name, reflecting its importance in Jewish tradition.
H0471I.emploi: Eliakim is mainly known as the son of Josiah whom Pharaoh Necho established as king of Judah around 609 B.C., replacing his older brother Jehoahaz. The Pharaoh gave him the name Jehoiakim to assert his control over the kingdom. This Eliakim/Jehoiakim reigned over Judah for eleven years, but under Egyptian and then Babylonian domination. Other men bearing the same name appear in the history of Hezekiah and in the account of the reconstruction of the Temple after the Babylonian exile.
H0471I.portee: This figure of Eliakim reminds us how the kingdoms of the earth depend on the powers that dominate them and how a name can be changed to signify a new political allegiance. For the believer, it shows that only God truly raises kings, and that changes of name or human destiny remain under His sovereignty.

sens: Wife of Aaron, mother of the priests of Israel
H0472.detail: Elisheba is the wife of the high priest Aaron and the mother of his four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. She belongs to a prominent family: she is the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, chief of the tribe of Judah. Through this marriage, she unites two of the highest lineages of the people, establishing the priestly dynasty of Israel. Her children Eleazar and Ithamar continued the service of the sanctuary after her (Exodus 6:23).
H0472.origine: The name Elisheba means "my God has sworn" or "God is an oath." It expresses a trust in God's commitment to Israel, particularly appropriate for one who would bear the priests responsible for maintaining the covenant between God and His people.
H0472.emploi: Elisheba appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 6:23, where she is introduced at the time of the genealogical composition of the tribes before the exodus from Egypt. This unique passage is sufficient to establish her major historical role: she is the founding mother of the priestly lineage. Although little mentioned by name, her importance is crucial, as all the priests and Levites who served God after her are descended from her sons.
H0472.portee: Elisheba reminds us that God places His servants in specific families and contexts to fulfill His plan. Her story also shows that the role of women in the faith of Israel is fundamental: a mother can be the foundation of an entire generation of servants of God. For the believer, she illustrates how God prepares future generations through the unions He blesses.

sens: Son of Javan and grandson of Noah in the genealogy of nations
H0473G.detail: Elischa is a character mentioned only in the genealogical lists of the Bible. He is the son of Javan, himself the son of Shem and grandson of Noah. He appears in the two passages that list Noah's descendants after the Flood: in Genesis 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:7. With his brothers Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim, he represents one of the branches of Noah's descendants and illustrates the multiplication of peoples on earth after the Flood.
H0473G.origine: The name Elischa literally means "God of the coming one" or "God of the one who comes." Like the other names in this genealogy, it may designate an eponymous ancestor — that is, an ancestor who gave his name to a people or region. Some scholars have conjectured that Elischa could be related to the Aeolians of ancient Greece, but ancient sources on this point remain uncertain.
H0473G.emploi: Elischa appears only twice in the Bible, both times in official genealogical lists: Genesis 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:7. These two passages list the sons of Javan in the same order. This name belongs to the table of nations that enumerates Noah's descendants after the Flood and divides the known peoples of the ancient world according to their presumed genealogy. Elischa is never the subject of an action or specific narrative; he remains a purely genealogical figure, comparable to the other names in this enumeration.

sens: Mediterranean coastal region, probably the island of Cyprus or its surroundings
Maritime trading people or group
Ancient name of a region producing dyed fabrics
H0473H.detail:
1. Elischa designates a region or island of the eastern Mediterranean, most likely ancient Cyprus. It is a coastal region from which valuable fabrics originated (Ezekiel 27:7).
2. It is also the name of a maritime people or civilization, known for its luxury trade and refined textile productions.
3. In the biblical context of Tyre's trade, Elischa represents a prestigious trading partner, supplier of blue and purple dyed fabrics, the most precious and costly colors of antiquity.
H0473H.origine: Elischa is a Hebrew proper name that literally means "God of the coming one" or "God of the one who comes." According to tradition, Elischa would have been a descendant of Noah, son of Javan. The name likely first designated a people, then the region or island that this people inhabited, particularly Cyprus. It is a typical example of how ancient peoples named the lands they occupied.
H0473H.emploi: Elischa appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:7, in the poetic and detailed description of the commercial wealth of the city of Tyre at its peak. The prophet lists Tyre's partners and suppliers, and Elischa is mentioned as a supplier of precious fabrics dyed in blue and purple. This passage shows that the region of Elischa was renowned throughout the ancient Levant for the exceptional quality of its textile productions, making it a major commercial center.
H0473H.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of international trade in biblical antiquity and how the riches of this world seduced peoples and led them to pride. The mention of Elischa in the context of Tyre's condemnation invites us to reflect on the futility of material goods and not to place our trust in earthly riches.

sens: Son of David and Bathsheba, brother of Solomon
H0474.detail: Elishua is one of the sons of David, born of his wife Bathsheba. He appears in the list of children born to David in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 14:5). Although mentioned among the twelve sons listed, the Bible does not report any particular events from his life.
H0474.origine: The name Elishua means "my God is wealth" or "God is salvation." It is formed from two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "Shua" (salvation or wealth), a typical structure of the theophoric names given in the royal family of David. In 1 Chronicles 3:6, he is also called Elishama, showing that these two names refer to the same person.
H0474.emploi: Elishua is mentioned only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages that list the sons of David born in Jerusalem: 2 Samuel 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 14:5. These royal lists provide no information about his personal role or destiny. It is a purely genealogical mention, without any associated narrative or action.

sens: son of Eljoenaï, from the royal lineage of Judah
H0475G.detail: 1. Éliaschib is a descendant of David mentioned in the genealogy of the kings of Judah. He is the son of Eljoenaï and is part of the list of seven children enumerated in 1 Chronicles 3:24 — a list that shows how the royal house of Judah branched out after the exile.
H0475G.origine: The name Éliaschib means "God restores" or "God reinstates" (from אל "God" and the verb שׁיב "to return, restore"). This name evokes the hope of restoration, particularly fitting for a descendant of the Judean royalty after the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile.
H0475G.emploi: Éliaschib appears only once in common French translations, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, as the son of Eljoenaï and a member of the royal lineage of Judah. The text cites him among seven brothers (Hodavia, Pelaja, Akkub, Jochanan, Delaja, and Anani), all from the same father. This genealogical passage preserves the memory of the continuation of the Davidic line beyond the exile. Historically, the name Éliaschib was borne by several important figures (notably a high priest during the time of Nehemiah and a temple singer), but the entry presented here concerns only this specific royal descendant from 1 Chronicles 3:24.

sens: priest during the time of King David
H0475H.detail: 1. Éliaschib is a priest who serves during the time of King David.
