He appears in the list of chief priestly families established by David, where he holds the eleventh rank in the cycle of service at the temple (1 Chronicles 24:12). Like all priests of that time, he was from the tribe of Levi and responsible for ensuring regular worship at the tabernacle.
H0475H.origine: The name Éliaschib literally means "God restores" or "God reinstates." It is composed of the Hebrew word for God (El) and a verb that evokes restoration or renewal. This name reflects the Hebrews' trust in God's faithfulness to preserve and maintain His people.
H0475H.emploi: Éliaschib appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:12, in the context of the organization of the priestly service established by King David. David instituted a system where the priests were divided into twenty-four groups that alternated service at the temple according to a regular rotation. Éliaschib leads the eleventh group, indicating that he was a person of respectable rank among the priests of his time.

sens: Priest and important man at the time of the return from exile, father of Jochanan
H0475I.detail: Éliaschib is a figure mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:6. He is the father of Jochanan, in whose chamber the prophet Ezra withdraws to weep over the sins of the people returned from exile. His name means "God restores," reflecting the hope of restoration that characterizes this time of return to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity.
H0475I.origine: The name Éliaschib combines two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and a verbal form meaning "to restore" or "to reinstate." This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among priestly families and descendants of David. The name expresses faith in God's ability to restore His people and His worship after disasters.
H0475I.emploi: Éliaschib appears only once in the preserved Bible, in Ezra 10:6. He is presented as the father of Jochanan and seems to hold a position of prestige in Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile, as his chamber is significant enough for the prophet Ezra to withdraw there. The context shows a moment of intercession and repentance of the people in light of the mixed marriages contracted during the exile.
H0475I.portee: This name reminds us that even secondary characters in biblical history bear names that confess faith in God. The moment when Ezra withdraws to the chamber of Éliaschib symbolizes the necessity of intercession and repentance in the restoration of God's people, a central theme of the book of Ezra.

sens: Man of the exile and return period
Temple singer who took a foreign wife
H0475J.detail:
1. Éliaschib is a man who lived during the time of the exile and the return of Israel, that is, in the sixth century before Christ, during the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity.
2. In the context of Ezra 10:24, Éliaschib is mentioned as one of the temple singers who had taken a foreign wife (non-Israelite). Following Ezra's decree against mixed marriages, he was among those who had to separate from their foreign wives to remain faithful to the law of Moses.
H0475J.origine: The name Éliaschib literally means "God restores" or "God reinstates." It comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of divine restoration and reinstatement. This name was borne by several important figures at different times in Israel's history: a priest during the time of King David, a royal descendant of David, and especially an influential high priest during the time of Nehemiah. The name expresses the messianic hope of the people restored by God.
H0475J.emploi: Éliaschib appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:24. He is mentioned as a temple singer who married a foreign woman. This passage is part of the account of the crisis of mixed marriages that the people returning from exile had contracted, which was contrary to the law. Ezra convened the assembly to correct this situation, and Éliaschib was among the pious men who agreed to separate from their foreign wives to obey the Torah and preserve the purity of worship.
H0475J.portee: This account reminds the reader of the importance of separation from evil and faithfulness to the word of God, even at the cost of painful personal sacrifices. For the early generations returning from exile, these mixed marriages represented a risk of slipping into idolatry. The mention of Éliaschib invites reflection on the difficult but necessary obedience that God requires of His people to remain holy and set apart.

sens: Man of the exile and return period
Son of the family of Zattu who married a foreign woman
H0475K.detail: Éliaschib is a name borne by several individuals at different times in Israel's history. In this specific usage (Ezra 10:27), he is a man from the family of Zattu who lived at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned among those who had contracted marriages with foreign women and who had to repudiate them at Ezra's command to preserve the purity of the people returned to the Promised Land.
H0475K.origine: The name Éliaschib comes from the Hebrew אֱלִישִׁיב composed of אֱל ("God") and שׁיב ("to restore"), which literally means "God restores." It is a common theophoric name in the genealogies of Israel, expressing trust in God's redemptive action. Several personalities in the Old Testament bear this name at different periods.
H0475K.emploi: Éliaschib appears only once in this passage of Ezra 10:27, in the list of those who had taken foreign wives during the exile and who consented to separate from them. This context shows that it was a strict measure taken at the time of the return to maintain separation from surrounding peoples. Although the source definition mentions other Éliaschib (a priest under David, a descendant of David, a high priest during Nehemiah's time, a temple singer), this entry concerns only the character from Ezra 10:27.
H0475K.portee: This account reminds the reader that the period of the return from exile was marked by tensions between religious fidelity and human ties. It illustrates the determination of the restored community to maintain its distinction and consecration to God after the exile, even at the cost of painful personal sacrifices. It is a testimony to the grace of God who restores (as the name itself signifies), but also to the responsibility of the people towards their covenant.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Ephraim during the time of the desert
Descendant of Ammihud and father of Nun
H0476G.detail: Élischama is a leader of the tribe of Ephraim who lived during the time of the Exodus and the desert wanderings. He is mentioned as the leader of his people during the census in Numbers 1:10, and he is among the princes who organize the camp and the sacrifices during the Exodus. His name means "My God has heard" and reflects confidence in divine protection. Through the genealogy reported in 1 Chronicles 7:26, we see that he is the son of Ammihud and the father of Nun, placing him in a prominent lineage of Ephraimites.
H0476G.origine: The name Élischama comes from Hebrew and literally means "My God has heard" (Eli = my God, Shama = has heard). This theophoric composition (incorporating the name of God) is common in Hebrew names and expresses the confidence that the Lord listens to prayer. The name belongs to a prestigious family of Ephraimites, as shown by its genealogy.
H0476G.emploi: Élischama appears six times in the Bible, all occurrences designating him as the leader of Ephraim during the time of the desert. In Numbers 1:10, he is named leader during the first census of the Israelites. In Numbers 2:18 and 10:22, he commands the army of Ephraim during the movements of the camp. In Numbers 7:48 and 7:53, he is among the princes who offer the inauguration sacrifices of the Tabernacle. The mention in 1 Chronicles 7:26 places him back in the genealogy of the sons of Ephraim, father of Nun. These six uses all converge on the same person: a prestigious and faithful leader during the time of Moses.
H0476G.portee: This leader represents responsible and faithful authority that participates in the major milestones of the life of the chosen people: the census, military organization, collective worship. His example encourages the believer to see that even human leaders are counted and recorded by God, and that they have a specific role to play in the walk of God's people.

sens: Son of David and Bathsheba, one of the twelve women with whom David had children in Jerusalem
H0476H.detail: 1. Élischama is one of the sons that King David had with various women during his reign in Jerusalem. He is mentioned among the children born from David's marriage to Bathsheba, after the birth of Solomon. His name means "My God has heard," reflecting a prayer or a confession of faith from the father. He appears in the genealogical lists of 2 Samuel 5:16 and Chronicles, where the twelve sons of David born in Jerusalem are enumerated.
H0476H.origine: The name Élischama is composed of two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "shama" (to hear, to listen). It thus means "My God has heard" or "God has listened." It is a theophoric name, that is, one that carries the name of God, common in ancient Israel. This type of name expresses confidence in God and acknowledges His intervention in human affairs, particularly at the birth of a child.
H0476H.emploi: Élischama is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in genealogical lists from the reign of David. He appears in 2 Samuel 5:16 among the children born in Jerusalem, then in 1 Chronicles 3:8 and 1 Chronicles 14:7, where Chronicles enumerate his eleven brothers. These passages show that Élischama was one of the twelve sons of King David with different women, illustrating the political and dynastic importance of David at that time. No specific act or event is reported about him in the biblical text.

sens: Man of the royal house of Judah during the divided monarchy
Father of Nethania, leader of a revolt against Gedaliah
H0476I.detail:
1. Élischama is a figure from the kingdom of Judah who lived at the time when the kingdom was collapsing under Babylonian attacks. His name means "my God has heard" in Hebrew. He is mentioned as a man of royal lineage, indicating that he descends from the royal family of David.
2. He is known as the father of Nethania, who leads a bloody political conspiracy: Nethania assassinates the governor Gedaliah and the men who accompany him (2 Kings 25:25 and Jeremiah 41:1). Through his son, Élischama is thus involved in one of the last revolts against the Babylonian power that then dominates Judah.
H0476I.origine: The name Élischama is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Eli" ("my God") and "Shama" ("has heard"). It belongs to a family of theophoric names—names that invoke the name or actions of God—that are very common among the Hebrews. The meaning of the name expresses the confidence that parents placed in God to listen and respond.
H0476I.emploi: Élischama appears twice in the Bible, only in the accounts of the fall of Jerusalem and its immediate aftermath. In both passages (2 Kings 25:25 and Jeremiah 41:1), he is designated as the father of Nethania and as a member of the royal lineage. These two parallel mentions recount the same event: the assassination of Gedaliah by Nethania, son of Élischama. The historical context is that of 586 B.C., shortly after the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem by the Babylonians.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H0476J.detail: Élischama is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is the son of Jekamja and belongs to the lineage of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:41). His name means "my God has heard," expressing confidence in divine listening.
H0476J.origine: The name Élischama is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Eli" (my God) and "Shama" (has heard). It reflects a common theological conviction in the Old Testament: that of a God who hears and responds to the prayers of His people. Several other characters bear this same name in the Old Testament, including an Ephraimite leader, a son of King David, and a secretary of King Jehoiakim.
H0476J.emploi: Élischama appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:41, in a genealogical list of the clan of Judah. He is presented there as the son of Jekamja, in the line of descent passing through Shallum. This mention is purely genealogical and does not recount anything else about his life or actions.

sens: Priest who taught the Law during the divided monarchy
H0476K.detail: Élischama is a priest sent by King Jehoshaphat of Judah to teach the Law in the cities of the kingdom (2 Chronicles 17:8). His name means "my God has heard" in Hebrew. He is part of an official mission alongside other Levites and priests, tasked with instructing the people in the knowledge of God and His Word.
H0476K.origine: The name Élischama combines two Hebrew elements: "Eli" (my God) and "Shama" (has heard). It belongs to a family of theophoric names common in the Old Testament, where the name expresses a personal relationship with God. The Bible mentions several characters bearing this name at different periods in Israel's history, but this one is specifically identified as a teaching priest from the 9th century B.C.
H0476K.emploi: Élischama appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He is mentioned among the religious representatives sent by King Jehoshaphat to instruct the inhabitants of Judah. This mission shows the importance that the king placed on teaching God's Law and the role of priests and Levites in the spiritual formation of the people. The context reveals a period of religious reform in Judah.
H0476K.portee: The presence of Élischama and his colleagues reminds us that the teaching of God's Word was a central responsibility of priests and Levites. This shows the reader that the knowledge of the Law is not acquired by chance, but through deliberate instruction. It is an invitation to take seriously the learning of the Scriptures and to honor those whom God calls to teach His Word.

sens: the secretary of King Jehoiakim
H0476L.detail: Élischama is a character from the book of Jeremiah, active at the royal court of Judah at the time when the prophet Jeremiah sends his written message. His name literally means "my God has heard." In the three occurrences that mention him (Jeremiah 36:12, 20, 21), he appears as the secretary of King Jehoiakim, an influential man at court who has his own chamber in the royal palace. It is in this chamber that the scroll of Jeremiah is first deposited before being presented to the king.
H0476L.origine: The name Élischama is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Eli" (my God) and "shama" (has heard). It thus expresses a confession of faith: "my God has heard." This theophoric name (which carries the name of God) was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel, such as a son of King David and an Ephraimite leader, but this one is specifically the secretary of Jehoiakim.
H0476L.emploi: Élischama appears three times in chapter 36 of Jeremiah, all passages concerning the event where the prophet has his written message read at court. In Jeremiah 36:12, he is presented as one of the officials sitting in the secretary's chamber who first hears the reading of the scroll. In Jeremiah 36:20 and 36:21, he is explicitly called "the secretary" and his chamber is identified as the storage place for the manuscript. His role is that of a high-ranking administrator, having direct access to official documents and sitting among the king's advisors.

sens: son of David
Ephraimite leader
secretary of King Jehoiakim
priest teaching the Law
man of Judah
H0476M.detail: This name designates several people in the Old Testament. The most well-known is a son of King David, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:6 among his children born in Jerusalem. It is also the name of an Ephraimite leader who led the people in the wilderness (Numbers 1:10), a secretary or officer of King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 36:12), a priest who taught the Law to the people (2 Chronicles 17:8), and other men of Judah mentioned throughout the history of Israel.
H0476M.origine: The Hebrew name אֱלִישָׁמָע (Élischama) literally means "my God has heard." It is composed of two elements: אֱלִי (eli, "my God") and שׁמַע (shama, "has heard"). It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing the belief that Israel has a God who listens to the prayers and cries of His people. Several people bore this name at different periods in biblical history.
H0476M.emploi: Élischama is the name of several important figures in the Old Testament, which reflects its popularity among the Israelites. The most famous is the son of David mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:6, born in Jerusalem during his reign. Other Élischama played roles of responsibility: leader of the Ephraimite troops in the wilderness, influential secretary or officer at the royal court, and teaching priest. This name recurs across several generations and social backgrounds, showing that it was valued in prominent families of Israel.
H0476M.portee: This name reminds us that the God of Israel is a God who listens. For the Christian, it evokes the fundamental truth that God hears the prayers of His people and responds to those who seek Him. The different individuals bearing this name embody various vocations in service to God and His people — royalty, military leadership, administrative and priestly roles — showing that the call to serve God is addressed to all walks of life.

sens: The prophet who succeeded Elijah in Northern Israel
Son of Shaphat, from Abel-Mehola
The one anointed by Elijah to replace him
The servant of the Lord who performed miracles and signs
The advisor to the kings of Israel during the divided kingdom
H0477.detail:
1. Élisée is the great prophet of Northern Israel who received the prophetic ministry from Elijah (2 Kings 2:9-12). He asked for a "double portion" of Elijah's spirit and succeeded his master after his ascension to heaven.
2. He was the son of Shaphat, a hardworking man from Abel-Mehola, a fertile region in Jordan (1 Kings 19:16). Elijah found him plowing in the fields and designated him for his service.
3. The Lord commanded Elijah to anoint him as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19:16), an act that formally consecrated him to divine ministry.
4. Élisée performed many remarkable miracles: he healed Naaman of leprosy (2 Kings 5:9-10), resurrected the son of the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4:32-35), multiplied the oil (2 Kings 4:1-7), and even after his death brought a dead man back to life (2 Kings 13:20-21).
5. He was the servant and advisor to the kings of Israel, notably Joram and Jehu (2 Kings 3:14, 6:19-20), and guided his contemporaries with his prophetic words and wisdom.
H0477.origine: The Hebrew name אֱלִישָׁע (Élisée) literally means "God is salvation" or "My God saves." It expresses trust in divine deliverance. This name reflects the prophet's mission: to manifest the saving power of the Lord through his signs and wonders among the people of Israel.
H0477.emploi: Élisée appears 52 times in the Bible, primarily in the second book of Kings (2 Kings 2-13). He carries out his ministry during the time of the divided monarchy, under several kings of Israel. The biblical account details his calling by Elijah (1 Kings 19:16-19), his experience of succession after Elijah's ascension (2 Kings 2), and his many miracles that confirmed his status as a prophet of the Lord. He advises kings, secures victory over the Syrians, and intervenes for both the common people and the great: he multiplies a widow's oil, heals Naaman the king of Syria, and presides over healings and resurrections. His ministry spans several decades and covers the entire public life of the Northern Israelite people.
H0477.portee: The life of Élisée teaches the reader that God chooses and equips His witnesses, even among simple workers, and that He performs wonders to deliver and restore. His example shows that prophetic faithfulness persists even when the people stray from God, and that the Lord remains the savior (as his name proclaims) in every circumstance. His miracles attest to the reality of divine power and invite the believer to trust the living God in every distress.

sens: Captain of the troops during the divided monarchy of Israel
H0478.detail: Élischaphath is a military leader who acts under the authority of the high priest Jehoiada in the 7th century BCE. His name, composed of the word for God and the verb to judge, literally means "My God has judged." He is one of the captains of hundreds who, along with Jehoiada, participates in the revolt against Queen Athaliah to restore the young king Joash to the throne of Judah (2 Chronicles 23:1). This man represents those military officers faithful to the Lord who, in times of political disorder, side with justice and legitimacy.
H0478.origine: The name Élischaphath comes from three Hebrew roots: Elohim (God), cha (possessive: my), and Shaphat (he has judged). It is a typical theophoric name in the Old Testament, where a person's name expresses a declaration of faith or relationship to the divine. The verb shaphat (to judge) is used throughout the Bible to express the action of rendering justice or deciding between good and evil.
H0478.emploi: Élischaphath appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 23:1. He is mentioned as the son of Zicri and one of the five captains of hundreds who unite with the high priest Jehoiada. This passage recounts the decisive moment when these officers, having recognized the injustice of Athaliah's reign and the legitimacy of young Joash, decide to restore order and law in Judah. His appearance at the top of the list suggests his importance or particular authority among these commanders.
H0478.portee: Élischaphath embodies the role of men in power who choose to serve justice and the will of God rather than personal ambition or tyranny. His commitment alongside Jehoiada shows that true strength lies in alliance with the Lord and His legitimate representatives. For the modern reader, he reminds us that positions of authority must be exercised according to the principles of justice that God establishes.

sens: This (demonstrative referring to a thing or person close in context)
These (plural of the demonstrative)
We, one (specific usage in biblical Aramaic)
H0479.detail:
1. The word designates something or someone specific, often already mentioned or present in the situation: "this city" (Ezra 4:21), "this house of God" (Ezra 6:8). It's like pointing with a finger: "this one, this one here".
2. In the plural, it refers to several people or things: "these elders of the Jews" (Ezra 6:8), "these men" (Daniel 3:27). The context shows exactly who is being referred to.
3. In Aramaic, this word can also take on the meaning of "we" or "one" in certain idiomatic usages: "we have inquired" (Ezra 5:9), "we will not find" (Daniel 6:5). This is a peculiarity of this language, less common than the demonstrative meaning.
H0479.origine: This word comes from the demonstrative Aramaic root אִל (il), related to the Hebrew אֵל (el, "these"). It is a very ancient demonstrative element used to point or designate. In biblical Aramaic, as in Hebrew, it is a fundamental grammatical particle for showing what one is talking about.
H0479.emploi: The word appears 13 times, only in the Aramaic passages of Daniel and Ezra (4:21 to 6:24), as it is Aramaic, the language used in these late administrative and historical accounts. It functions as a simple demonstrative: to designate a person, a group, or a thing that the text has just mentioned or that will be clarified. In the lists of persecutors (Daniel 3 and 6), it helps to identify the conspirators: "these men"; in the decrees of the king (Ezra 4 to 6), it shows which building or group is being referred to. It is a neutral and very common tool for textual clarity.

sens: Exclamation of despair or lamentation
Cry in the face of a hopeless situation
Call placed upon oneself or the world
H0480.detail:
1. The word is an interjection that the speaker utters as a sign of despair. It expresses deep affliction, often when one feels overwhelmed. Job cries it out in Job 10:15 while he is suffering intensely: "If I am guilty, woe to me!" — it is the cry of a broken heart.
2. It is also a groan in the face of absurdity or deprivation. The prophet Micah utters it in Micah 7:1 upon seeing that there is nothing good to harvest: "Woe to me! for there are no clusters to eat" — the word conveys the bitterness of one who finds only disappointment.
3. More broadly, it is a lamentation: the one who utters it calls down woe upon himself or his condition, like a cry to God or to nothingness, confessing his powerlessness.
H0480.origine: The Hebrew word אַלְלַי is an interjection that expresses raw emotion, not derived from a clear verbal root. It belongs to the family of cries of pain and lamentation in Hebrew, like other similar exclamations. Its meaning has not changed: it has always been a voice of affliction, arising from suffering.
H0480.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. Both usages occur in moments of great personal distress: Job in the midst of his inexplicable sufferings, and Micah the prophet contemplating the spiritual ruin of his people. In both cases, it is a cry uttered to express an affliction that cannot be contained: not a reproach directed at someone, but a confession of powerlessness and pain.
H0480.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide despair and suffering. It allows the righteous to cry out their pain, as Job does before God. It is a word for those going through trials who need their tears, their inner revolt against injustice or absurdity to be recognized as legitimate. God listens to the one who cries "woe" while even in their complaint there is a form of prayer.

sens: who does not speak, who remains silent
who cannot speak, deprived of speech
to bind, to attach (rare original meaning)
H0481.detail:
1. To be mute is to remain voiceless, unable or refusing to speak. It is the silence of the prisoner, the defeated, or one who accepts their fate without protest. The prophet Ezekiel receives the command: "I will bind your tongue to your palate, so that you will be mute" (Ezekiel 3:26), an image of a mouth closed by the will of God.
2. Muteness can be a choice: one who prefers to remain silent rather than defend their cause or respond to insults. The Psalmist says, "I was mute, in silence" (Psalms 39:3), accepting his suffering without complaint. It is also the attitude of the suffering Servant in Isaiah: "Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that is mute before its shearers; he did not open his mouth" (Isaiah 53:7).
3. The etymological meaning of the word refers to the idea of binding or attaching, as in the expression "binding sheaves" (Genesis 37:7). It is this binding that renders one mute: the tongue tied to the palate, the man bound and defenseless.
H0481.origine: The Hebrew verb אָלַם comes from a root that primarily evokes the act of binding, of attaching firmly. From there arises the meaning of remaining silent: one who is bound cannot speak. The root also appears in other Hebrew forms denoting silence or the inability to express oneself. It is a concrete word that has become an image of subjugation and non-resistance.
H0481.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, always in relation to silence or the inability to speak. The Psalms use it to express the choice of silence in the face of suffering or lies: "lying lips" must become "mute" (Psalms 31:19), and the faithful "remains mute" before the Lord (Psalms 39:3, 39:10). Isaiah 53:7 places it on the lips of the suffering Servant, a messianic image of one who endures without defending himself. Ezekiel uses it for a silence imposed by God on the prophet himself (Ezekiel 3:26), and then for the moment when his mouth finally opens after judgment (Ezekiel 24:27, Ezekiel 33:22). Only one usage retains the concrete meaning of binding (Genesis 37:7).
H0481.portee: This word teaches that silence in the face of injustice is not weakness, but sometimes wisdom or obedience. The suffering Servant who remains mute becomes a figure of one who entrusts his defense to God rather than to human words. For the believer, it is an invitation to listen rather than protest, to accept God's will even when it comes through suffering.

sens: State of one who does not speak, who refrains from speaking
Voluntary abstention from words, chosen mutism
Tranquility without noise or speech
H0482.detail:
1. Silence is the absence of speech, the act of saying nothing. It is the attitude of one who holds back their voice and remains mute. In Psalms 58:2, the psalmist asks the judges: "Do you really render justice by keeping silent?" — he confronts them about their inaction, their refusal to speak up for what is right.
2. It is also a voluntary abstention, a choice not to speak when one could or should. Silence can be a fault (here, the silence of the judges in the face of injustice), or conversely, a virtue (keeping silent rather than uttering vain or sinful words).
3. The word more broadly evokes the absence of noise and movement, a silent tranquility, the state of one who refrains not only from speaking but from any agitation.
H0482.origine: The Hebrew word אֵלֶם (élem) comes from a root meaning "to be mute" or "to be deaf." It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that describe inaction or voluntary stillness. In the Greek Old Testament, it can be rendered by the Greek σιωπή (siôpê), which has the same connotation: silence as the state of one who does not speak.
H0482.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 58:2, in a context of reproach directed at the judges. The psalmist indignantly asks if these magistrates truly render justice "in silence," that is, by remaining inert, without intervening to right wrongs. It is thus a culpable silence, a blameworthy passivity in the face of evil and injustice. The word emphasizes that silence is never neutral: when it comes to defending justice, the absence of speech becomes complicity.
H0482.portee: This word reminds the reader that silence has a moral value. Keeping silent when one should speak up to defend the weak or justice is a sin of omission. Conversely, it also invites reflection on our own silences: do we speak when we should, or do we hide behind a false discretion? For the Christian, it is a call not to remain mute in the face of oppression and injustice.

sens: Who cannot speak or does not speak
Who remains silent, who makes no noise
Unable to communicate or express oneself
Idol or object without power or life
H0483.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: a mute person cannot produce speech. In Exodus 4:11, God asks Moses, "Who makes one mute?" — it is the Lord who created even those who are deprived of speech. The mute is one who lacks the use of speech.

2. The word also designates one who chooses silence, who refrains from speaking. In Psalms 38:14, the psalmist says, "I am like a mute, who does not open his mouth": he suffers but remains silent, refusing to complain or respond.

3. In a figurative sense, it is the absence of voice, the inability to express oneself or to be heard. Proverbs 31:8 calls to "open your mouth for the mute," meaning to speak up for those who cannot defend themselves.

4. The word also applies to idols or lifeless objects: in Habakkuk 2:18, the mute idols cannot speak or act. It is the image of total powerlessness.
H0483.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be bound" or "tied," hence the idea of a closed mouth, unable to open. The basic image is obstruction or closure. This word can also be associated with the notion of silence that envelops one who does not speak.
H0483.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always with an emotional or religious charge. It first designates the mute as unfortunate or disadvantaged: Exodus 4:11 reminds us that God is responsible even for disabilities; Psalms 38:14 expresses silent suffering; Proverbs 31:8 urges justice for the mute. In the context of messianic restoration, Isaiah 35:6 announces that "the tongue of the mute will sing for joy" — the mute will regain speech as a sign of divine salvation. Isaiah 56:10 describes the mute dogs (the watchmen) as useless, unable to defend. Habakkuk 2:18 qualifies the idols as mute, emphasizing their emptiness.
H0483.portee: This word reminds us of the dignity of all, including the most vulnerable, and the call to be their voice. In Jesus, the mute regains the use of speech — Matthew 12:22 recounts that a mute demoniac was brought to Jesus, and he healed him. It is a sign of the Kingdom: the Messiah restores the voice to one who has lost it. This invites the Christian to work for justice and to recognize that only God has power over life and death, speech and silence.

sens: Precious wood imported from the East, probably from Lebanon or Ophir
Luxury material used for construction and musical instruments
H0484.detail:
1. Sandalwood is a rare and precious wood that the Phoenician ships of Hiram brought from Ophir, a distant and rich region. It is an eastern material, valued for its quality and rarity (1 Kings 10:11).
2. This precious wood was used to make high-value objects: King Solomon made balustrades (or staircases) for the temple of the Lord and for his palace, as well as harps and lyres for the worship musicians. Its rarity was such that after Solomon's imports, "no more sandalwood came to Israel" (1 Kings 10:12).
H0484.origine: The Hebrew word אַלְמֻגִּים (almugim) designates a type of exotic wood, probably sandalwood or a similar essence from Lebanon or the East. Its exact etymology remains debated among scholars, but it is a term for a rare material brought by long-distance trade. The Segond translates this rare word as "sandal" or "sandalwood," highlighting its precious and distant character.
H0484.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Kings 10, in the account of King Solomon's prosperous trade. Hiram's ships (king of Tyre) brought it from Ophir along with gold and precious stones, indicating that sandalwood was classified among the most sought-after royal treasures. Solomon used it to adorn his temple and palace, and to make liturgical musical instruments, revealing its exclusively royal and religious use in ancient Israel.
H0484.portee: This precious wood reminds us of the wealth and wisdom granted to King Solomon, as well as his commitment to magnify the worship of the God of Israel. Its absence after the Solomonic era underscores that even the most extraordinary earthly riches last only a time and that no human prosperity is eternal. For the believer, it is an invitation not to seek security in material goods, however precious they may be.

sens: Bundle of grains tied together after the harvest
Image of power and dominion (symbolic dream)
Fruit of labor and joy of the harvest
H0485.detail:
1. A sheaf is a bundle of grains — wheat, barley, or other grain — that is tied together after the ears have been cut in the field. It is the immediate result of the harvest, before the threshing. In Genesis 37:7, young Joseph dreams that he is binding sheaves in the field with his brothers, and his sheaf stands upright while theirs bow down before it.

2. In Joseph's dream, the sheaf becomes a symbolic image: his standing and revered sheaf represents his future dominion over his brothers and family. The dream figuratively announces that he will become the leader and that others will bow before him — which will indeed be fulfilled in Egypt.

3. In Psalms 126:6, the sheaf embodies the joy and reward of labor. He who sows while weeping — in pain and effort — returns rejoicing, carrying his sheaves, a symbol of the abundance gained and the divine blessing on his labor.
H0485.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "binding" or "assembling." A sheaf is grain gathered and tied into a tight bundle. This simple image of agricultural work has allowed the biblical text to use it as a symbol: a raised sheaf signifies a power that rises; sheaves that bow down signify submission. The context of the ancient Near East, where agriculture was central, makes this image vivid and understandable to all.
H0485.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in contexts heavily laden with symbolism. In Genesis 37:7, Joseph recounts his harvest dream to his family: he and his brothers are binding sheaves, and his stands upright while the others bow down. It is a prophetic dream announcing Joseph's exaltation over his family. In Psalms 126:6, the sheaf is the image of the joyful harvest that rewards the patient sower: he who weeps while sowing returns with joy, carrying his sheaves. In both cases, the sheaf represents an accomplishment: either a power asserting itself or a concrete blessing.
H0485.portee: The sheaf reminds us that our efforts and tears are not in vain. He who labors in faith — who sows while weeping — will reap with joy. The story of Joseph also shows that God elevates those He chooses and that even present humiliations do not contradict divine promises. The sheaf symbolizes hope: the promise transforms difficult labor into certainty of harvest.

sens: Son of Joktan, ancestor of the Arab peoples
H0486.detail: Almodad is a man living in the time of the Patriarchs, son of Joktan and brother of Sheba, Ophir, and other ancestors of peoples and regions of the Middle East and Arabia. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Shem (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20).
H0486.origine: His name means "unmeasured" or "one who does not measure." It is a Hebrew name formed in the pattern of other names from the same generation, all descendants of Noah through Shem and Joktan.
H0486.emploi: Almodad appears twice in the Bible, only in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:26 and in 1 Chronicles 1:20, where he opens the list of the twelve sons of Joktan. These lists trace the peoples descended from Noah after the Flood and indicate the ancestors of the Arab nations and the Middle East. Almodad is presented as the firstborn of Joktan.

sens: City in the territory of Asher
H0487.detail: Allammelech is a location in Asher, a tribe of Israel in the north, mentioned in the allotment of the promised land. Its name literally means "oak of the king," perhaps because a famous large oak marked the site or because the region was under royal administration.
H0487.origine: The Hebrew name Allammelech is composed of two elements: al (oak, a strong and majestic tree) and melek (king). This composition of place names from concrete words and terms of power is common in ancient Canaan. The oak was an imposing and sacred tree, often associated with important places or divine revelations in the Bible.
H0487.emploi: Allammelech appears only once in the Bible, during the description of the boundaries of the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:26). It is listed among a enumeration of border cities, between Carmel and Shichor-Libnath, placing the site in the northern coastal region of Palestine. Its unique mention suggests that it was a known locality at the time of writing, but of secondary importance.

sens: Left alone, without support
Deprived of the one who accompanied them
Forgotten, abandoned by their God
H0488.detail:
1. The word describes someone who has lost the one they relied on — like a widow who no longer has her husband to protect her. In Jeremiah 51:5, the prophet asserts that Israel and Judah are not "forsaken" by their God: they are not left alone in the face of threats, for the Lord of hosts remains their support.
2. The image broadens in a figurative sense: to be forsaken means to be left to oneself, without the presence or help of the one who should be there. It is the experience of one who feels forgotten at the moment when they most need not to be forgotten.
3. Applied to Israel, the word carries a strong spiritual charge: it is less about a physical absence than about a rupture of the covenant, a withdrawal of divine protection. The context of Jeremiah reassuring Israel that their God has not forsaken them shows that this word touches on the question of salvation and God's faithfulness.
H0488.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root that designates the widow — one who remains alone after the death of a spouse. The central image is thus that of forced solitude, the absence of the one who was a protector. This root is linked to mourning and disarray, to the condition of vulnerability of one who has no one to rely on.
H0488.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Jeremiah 51:5). Although rare, its use is significant: it appears in an oracle where the prophet contrasts the two peoples — Israel and Judah — and the enemy nation, the Chaldeans. Jeremiah declares that Israel is not forsaken by their God, while the land of the Chaldeans is filled with crimes. This contrast shows that the word carries a religious value: being forsaken by God would be a sign of condemnation, while not being forsaken affirms the maintenance of the covenant.
H0488.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of being forgotten by God is a constant temptation for the believer, especially in trials. The assurance that God does not forsake us is a word of comfort in the moments when we feel alone. It invites the reader to discern between the feeling of abandonment and the reality of divine faithfulness, which persists even when everything seems against us.

sens: the state of a woman deprived of her husband by death
the pain and vulnerability of one who has lost her spouse
H0489.detail:
1. Widowhood is the condition of a woman whose husband has died. It is the civil and social status of the widow, who finds herself deprived of the protection and support of her husband. In Isaiah 47:9, the Lord announces to Babylon that she will experience widowhood, meaning she will lose her power and security, just as a woman loses her protector.
2. Widowhood also evokes moral suffering and precariousness: the widow finds herself alone in facing trials, without the one who should have defended her and provided for her needs. This is why widowhood symbolizes misfortune and affliction, used here to describe the terrible punishment that will befall Babylon.
H0489.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses absence, lack. Widowhood is literally the state of being without a husband, a word formed from the same root as "widow." It is a term that describes a rupture: the one who was married finds herself alone, a particularly grave reality in ancient Israel, where marriage was the framework for a woman's social and economic status.
H0489.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 47:9. In this passage, the Lord addresses Babylon, the queen of empires, and announces to her two punishments that will come "suddenly, on the same day": the deprivation of children and widowhood. These two misfortunes symbolize the total fall of the Babylonian empire: loss of its descendants (thus its future) and loss of its protective strength (symbolized by the husband that represents power). The word is used in both a concrete and figurative sense, describing both the fate of the women of Babylon and that of the nation itself.
H0489.portee: Widowhood reminds every reader of the difficult fate of widows in the Bible: women without protection, often at the mercy of others. This explains the laws of the Old Testament that command to help them. But in this passage, the word also reminds us that even the greatest power — Babylon — does not escape God's judgment: she will experience weakness, abandonment, and suffering. It is a warning against pride and an assurance that God will ultimately defend His own.

sens: A woman whose husband has died
A woman without protection, left in misery
The people of Israel deprived of divine protection
H0490.detail:
1. A widow is a woman whose husband has passed away. In the Old Testament, this was a difficult condition: without a husband to provide for her needs, she risked poverty and exploitation. This is why Israelite law constantly addresses this issue: God commands not to oppress the widow (Exodus 22:22) and to allow her to glean in the fields after the harvest (Deuteronomy 24:19-21).
2. The word more broadly designates a woman in misfortune and without recourse. Job can say, "I brought joy to the heart of the widow" (Job 29:13) to show his generosity towards the underprivileged. It is the biblical image of one who has no one to defend them: an orphan and a widow are always cited together as the most vulnerable.
3. In the prophets, "widow" becomes an image of the people of Israel or Jerusalem abandoned by God. Isaiah 47:8 addresses Babylon: "You said: I will always be queen, and I will never experience widowhood" — God treats her as a widow without help.
H0490.origine: The Hebrew word almana comes from a root that suggests absence, solitude. Its equivalent in biblical Greek (chêra) carries the same idea: a woman alone. The family of the word refers to the state of isolation and fragility, which explains why Scripture emphasizes the duty to protect the widow — she represents the weak that no one helps.
H0490.emploi: The word "widow" appears 53 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Law (Deuteronomy) and the Prophets. There are three typical usages: first, the legal and social situation: the Law forbids oppressing the widow (Exodus 22:22) and commands including her in celebrations and the sharing of harvests (Deuteronomy 16:14, Deuteronomy 26:12-13). Next, the call to compassion: Job and the Psalms celebrate those who help the widow (Job 29:13; Psalms 146:9). Finally, the prophetic image: Jeremiah and Isaiah use "widow" to describe Jerusalem under God's judgment, deprived of her divine husband (Isaiah 1:23; Jeremiah 49:11).
H0490.portee: The figure of the widow reveals to the believer that God cares for the weak and the abandoned: "Father of the fatherless and defender of widows, it is God" (Psalms 68:6). Protecting the widow is not optional charity; it is a command that shows whether one truly loves God. For the Christian, this invites looking around: who are the "widows" of today, the isolated, the defenseless? God calls us to see in them the reflection of His heart.

sens: the state of a woman whose husband has died
the clothing or distinctive signs of mourning worn by a widow
the difficult and honorable social condition of a woman without a husband
abandonment or deprivation in misfortune
H0491.detail:
1. Widowhood is primarily the state of a woman who has lost her husband through death. In biblical culture, this is a situation that completely changes a woman's social status and future. Tamar, in Genesis 38:14, removes her "widow's garments" to deceive Judah: these clothes or this distinctive sign (perhaps a specific robe or veil) allowed everyone to recognize a woman in mourning.
2. By extension, widowhood designates the visible signs of mourning that a widow wears: the clothing, the veil, which mark her changed status. Tamar "put on her widow's garments" (Genesis 38:19) once her objective was achieved, showing that this costume was easily recognizable.
3. Widowhood can also evoke the social condition and vulnerability of a widow. David's ten concubines, confined and maintained but never visited (2 Samuel 20:3), are in a "state of widowhood": they live in expectation of a marital bond that will never be renewed.
4. Figuratively, widowhood symbolizes abandonment, deprivation, and misfortune. When God comforts Zion in Isaiah 54:4 by saying she will not forget "the reproach of her widowhood," He refers to the time of separation and suffering before restoration, as if Jerusalem were a wife temporarily abandoned.
H0491.origine: The Hebrew word אַלְמָנוּת comes from the root אָלַם which means to be silent, struck dumb — the idea being that the widow, in mourning and deprived of her protector, remains in silence and isolation. In Hebrew, "widow" is אַלְמָנָה, and "widowhood" is its abstract form designating the state or condition. This word reflects one of the most difficult realities of antiquity: a woman without a husband was exposed to poverty and abandonment.
H0491.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always in Hebrew with the same root. In Genesis 38, it designates the distinctive mourning garments that a woman would wear to signal her status. In 2 Samuel 20:3, it qualifies the condition of the royal concubines confined, living in a permanent "state of widowhood." In Isaiah 54:4, the prophet uses the word figuratively to describe the period of suffering of Jerusalem, separated from God like a wife from her husband. In all cases, widowhood refers to a loss, a rupture of connection, and social vulnerability.
H0491.portee: Widowhood in the Bible reminds us of the importance of protection and justice for the weakest. God is particularly concerned for widows and orphans, encouraging them to rely on His protection. This word invites the reader to compassion for those who are alone and destitute, and to see in God the one who rescues the abandoned.

sens: a person whose name is not mentioned or is intentionally left unspecified
a place or thing whose identity is not specified
H0492.detail:
1. The word designates a person without naming them, either because they have not yet been identified or because one chooses not to specify them. In Ruth 4:1, Boaz refers to 'such' a man whose role he knows well (the one who has the right of redemption), but does not state his name at that moment in the narrative: it is a way of speaking politely and formally, as if saying 'Mr. So-and-so.'
2. The word also applies to a place or situation without indicating the precise details. In 2 Kings 6:8, the king of Syria announces that his camp will be in 'such a place' without giving the exact location: the word expresses voluntary indeterminacy or imprecision.
H0492.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning 'to hide' or 'to mask.' It is formed on the idea of something that remains in the shadows, whose identity is not revealed. The word is part of expressions used to speak discreetly or veiled, as if keeping a secret or reserve.
H0492.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to designate a person or thing vaguely. In Ruth 4:1, Boaz uses it to refer to a man whom readers will later discover to be a close relative—this is a narrative technique: his name is not initially stated, he is called 'such.' In 1 Samuel 21:2 and 2 Kings 6:8, the word appears to indicate a matter or place without precision. In all cases, it marks a willingness not to name or to maintain a certain distance.
H0492.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible often speaks in concrete and situated terms: it does not hide names or facts, but sometimes reveals them gradually or presents them cautiously. For the reader, it is an invitation to trust the unfolding of the narrative and to recognize that the silences of the text are never trivial.

sens: man from the time of the divided monarchy, father of two of David's valiant warriors
H0493.detail: Elnaam is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when David reigns in divided Israel. He is known solely because he had two sons, Jeribaï and Joschavia, who were among David's renowned warriors—these powerful and loyal men formed the king's military elite (1 Chronicles 11:46).
H0493.origine: The name Elnaam literally means 'God is delight' or 'God is pleasant': it combines El (God) and the idea of joy or pleasure. It is a theophoric name, very common in ancient Jewish culture, expressing trust in God's goodness and kindness.
H0493.emploi: Elnaam appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 11:46, where he is presented as the father of Jeribaï and Joschavia. These two sons are listed among David's thirty-seven valiant warriors, a list of exceptional men who distinguished themselves by their courage and loyalty during the king's reign. The context shows that although Elnaam himself is not a noted warrior, his honor comes from his sons and their service to the king of Israel.

sens: man from Jerusalem, maternal grandfather of King Jehoiachin
H0494G.detail: 1. Elnathan is a notable from Jerusalem mentioned only in 2 Kings 24:8, where he is presented as the father of Nehuschtha, the mother of King Jehoiachin. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, at a time when the weakened kingdom of Judah faced Babylonian domination. His name means 'God has given,' which is a confession of faith inscribed in his own name.
H0494G.origine: The name Elnathan is composed of two Hebrew elements: El ('God') and nathan ('to give'). It expresses gratitude to God for a gift received, probably the birth or life of this child. This type of theophoric name, associating the divine name with an action or quality, is common in Israel and reflects the piety of the parents.
H0494G.emploi: Elnathan appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 24:8. He is identified as the father of Nehuschtha and thus the maternal grandfather of King Jehoiachin, who ascended to the throne of Judah at eighteen years old. This genealogical detail, which may seem minor, underscores the importance of family lineages in the royalty of Israel: even the grandparents of kings play a role in the history of salvation.

sens: Leader among the descendants of the exiles returned from Babylon, during the time of Ezra
H0494H.detail: 1. Elnathan is a Jewish leader who returns from Babylonian exile with Ezra. His name means 'God has given' in Hebrew. Ezra calls upon him to help gather the Levites and prepare for the return to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16).
H0494H.origine: The name Elnathan comes from two Hebrew elements: 'El' (God) and 'natan' (to give). It expresses trust in God's generosity, who gives His blessings to His people. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) is common in Israel to express gratitude to God.
H0494H.emploi: Elnathan appears in Ezra 8:16, where he is mentioned among the leaders that the scribe Ezra gathers to organize the return of the exiles from Babylon. His role is to help constitute a delegation responsible for bringing back to Jerusalem the offerings intended for the restored temple.

sens: Levitical leader of the return from exile, during the time of Ezra
H0494I.detail: Elnathan is a leader (or teacher of the Law) who returns from exile in Babylon with Ezra, around 458 B.C. His name means 'God has given' in Hebrew. He appears in the list of officials that Ezra summons to organize the return and to teach the Law in Jerusalem. He is one of the trusted men upon whom Ezra relies to restore the religious life of the people returned to the Promised Land.
H0494I.origine: The name Elnathan is composed of two Hebrew elements: El ('God') and nathan ('he has given'). It is a theophoric name that expresses gratitude to God for a gift received, particularly the birth of a child. Other characters with this name appear in Israel's history, including an official of King Jehoiachin and a military leader under Jehoiakim, but they are not the same person as the one mentioned here.
H0494I.emploi: Elnathan is mentioned only once in the preserved biblical usages, in Ezra 8:16. He appears in the list of leaders and teachers of the Law that Ezra gathers at the time of the return from exile. His inclusion in this enumeration alongside other names of officials indicates his religious and administrative authority among the repatriates. The context suggests that he played an important role in organizing and teaching the post-exilic community.

sens: Israeli leader of the return from exile with Ezra
Character mentioned as a teacher or master of the Law
H0494J.detail: 1. Elnathan is a leader or official among the Israelites who returned from Babylonian captivity with Ezra, probably in the 5th century B.C. (Ezra 8:16). 2. He also appears as a teacher, that is, a master or interpreter of the Mosaic Law, serving the restored community (Ezra 8:16).
H0494J.origine: The name Elnathan literally means 'God has given' in Hebrew, composed of El (God) and natan (to give). It is a common theophoric name in the Bible, expressing gratitude to God for a gift, particularly the birth of a child.
H0494J.emploi: Elnathan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:16, at the time when Ezra prepares the return of the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem. He is listed among both the summoned leaders and the teachers of the Law. His role suggests that he was a respected and educated figure in the Jewish community of the Persian period, tasked with guiding the people both administratively and spiritually.
H0494J.portee: The mention of Elnathan reminds us that the return from exile was not merely a material restoration: it required educated and pious men, leaders who combined civil responsibility with knowledge of God's Law. His name, 'God has given,' also expresses the conviction that after punishment, God continues to provide His people with the guides and strength they need to rise again.

sens: High-ranking figure under King Jehoiakim of Judah
H0494K.detail: Elnathan is an official of the royal court of Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim (early 6th century B.C.). His name means "God has given." He appears in the book of Jeremiah as an influential man: King Jehoiakim personally sends him to Egypt for an important mission, likely to seek the prophet Jeremiah or for a state matter (Jeremiah 26:22). He is also among the most important leaders of the kingdom, sitting in the king's secretary's chamber during the reading of the scroll of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 36:12), and he even shows courage by opposing the king who wants to burn this prophetic book (Jeremiah 36:25). He is a man of authority, but also someone who can recognize the word of God, even if the king does not heed his warnings.
H0494K.origine: The name Elnathan is composed of two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "natan" (to give). It literally means "God has given" or "God gives." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for a received gift, often the birth of a child.
H0494K.emploi: Elnathan is mentioned three times in the book of Jeremiah, all passages occurring between 605 and 604 B.C., a time of intense political turmoil in Judah. First sent to Egypt by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:22), he later reappears as one of the king's chief advisors, sitting on the royal council. His role evolves from a mere executor of royal orders to an influential advisor, as he dares to oppose the king's plan to destroy the prophetic scroll. This shows that Elnathan possessed a certain moral autonomy and a fear of God, even while remaining subject to the king's authority.
H0494K.portee: Elnathan illustrates how God can raise up, even in the courts of kings, men who dare to oppose bad decisions and who have respect for the divine word. His example invites the reader not to assume that all who live in luxury and power are closed to God, and to pray that authorities listen to those who warn them in the name of the Lord.

sens: Ancient city of Babylonia
Political power associated with a coalition against Abraham
H0495.detail:
1. Ellasar is an ancient city located in Babylonia, about 50 kilometers east of Ur. It appears in the account of Genesis 14 as the capital of Arioch, one of the four eastern kings who form a military coalition.
2. Historically, Ellasar represents a second-tier political power in Mesopotamia, significant enough to participate in a military expedition to the Near East (Genesis 14:1, 14:9), but subject to the hegemony of Kedorlaomer, king of Elam, who leads this coalition.
H0495.origine: The name means "God is the punisher" or "God is the chastiser." Ellasar is a historical city of ancient Babylonia, attested in Mesopotamian sources. Its name reflects the religious beliefs of the inhabitants of this region, where deities represented various functions and divine attributes.
H0495.emploi: Ellasar appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the account of Genesis 14, the only place where this ancient location is mentioned. It is found in verses 1 and 9, designating each time the kingdom of Arioch among the four allied kings. These two occurrences describe the same event: the formation of an alliance of Mesopotamian powers marching against the kings of the Near East.
H0495.portee: This passage illustrates the geopolitical context of ancient times and Abraham's position in relation to the great powers of the world. Although Abraham is a mere clan leader, he intervenes to rescue Lot and defeats a coalition of powerful kings, showing that Abraham's strength comes from his relationship with God and not from earthly military power.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim, living in the time of Egypt and the desert
H0496.detail: Élead is a man of the tribe of Ephraim mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:21. He is the son of Shuthalh and the brother of Zabad, Ezer, and others. According to the account, Élead and his brother Ezer were killed by the men of Gath who lived in the land, during an expedition to take livestock. This brief passage shows him as a member of the Ephraim family during ancient times, before the final settlement in Canaan.
H0496.origine: The name Élead means "God has testified" in Hebrew. It is composed of "El" (God) and "ad" (he has testified). The name expresses the belief that God testifies or intervenes. Élead belongs to the genealogy of the descendants of Ephraim, one of Joseph's sons.
H0496.emploi: Élead appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:21, where he is cited in the genealogical list of Ephraim. The passage describes an event where he and his brother Ezer were killed by the people of Gath during an attempt to steal livestock. This brief account illustrates the conflicts that could arise between tribes and the peoples established in Canaan during this ancient period.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim
Descendant of Ephraim in the royal genealogy
H0497.detail: 1. Éleada is a man belonging to the tribe of Ephraim, mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of this tribe during the divided monarchy. He appears in the list of descendants of Ephraim established during the time of King David and his successors. 2. In the genealogical line, Éleada is the son of Tachat and the father of another Tachat, which shows how names were repeated in the ancient families of Israel. This genealogy testifies to the continuity of the tribe of Ephraim through the generations.
H0497.origine: His name means "God has adorned" or "God has beautified," composed of two elements: "El" (God) and a root expressing the idea of beautifying or preparing. This name reflects the belief that God had beautified or prepared this child, a common practice in Hebrew onomastics where names expressed the parents' faith in divine providence.
H0497.emploi: Éleada is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:20, where he appears in the general genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. He appears as a link in a chain of generations, without any particular narrative concerning him or act that distinguishes him. This brief mention shows that some names are preserved in genealogical records even when no remarkable event is associated with them.

sens: Benjaminite warrior during the time of David
H0498.detail: Éluzaï is a warrior from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David during his refuge at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:5). He appears in the list of valiant men who rallied to David before his accession to the throne.
H0498.origine: The name Éluzaï means "God is my strength" or "God is my power." It combines the Hebrew word El (God) and uzay (strength, power), expressing confidence in divine power. It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, where the name proclaims a personal relationship with God.
H0498.emploi: Éluzaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:5, within a list of Benjaminite warriors who came to support David at Ziklag. This list enumerates the valiant men who recognized the divine anointing on David and came to support him before his official kingship.
H0498.portee: Éluzaï reminds us that many warriors known to God supported David, not by human calculation but by recognition of the divine work. His name bears witness to a personal faith in the power of God, a common value among the faithful warriors who followed the one chosen by God.

sens: Son of Aaron, priest who succeeded his father
Son of Abinadab, guardian of the ark of the covenant
Priest who restored the walls of Jerusalem during the time of Ezra
Warrior among David's mighty men
Levite
Member of the lineage of Parosh
H0499G.detail:
1. Eleazar is the son of the high priest Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23). After the death of his brothers Nadab and Abihu, consumed by divine fire for offering unauthorized incense, Eleazar becomes the chief assistant to his father Aaron in the service of the tabernacle. Upon Aaron's death, he succeeds him as the high priest of Israel (Deuteronomy 10:6). He accompanies Moses during the census of the people and plays a crucial role in organizing worship and distributing the land (Numbers 26:3, Numbers 27:19).

2. A man from the house of Abinadab, in Kiriath-Jearim, who was consecrated to guard the ark of the covenant for several years.

3. A priest who, under the governor Ezra, participated in the restoration and dedication of the walls of Jerusalem.

4. One of the renowned warriors of King David, mentioned among his mighty men.

5. A Levite serving in the temple.

6. A descendant of the lineage of Parosh, mentioned in the genealogies.
H0499G.origine: The name Eleazar means "God has helped" or "God helps" in Hebrew, composed of "El" (God) and "Azar" (to help). It is a typical theophoric name in the Semitic world, expressing divine intervention. The family of Aaron and his descendants bear several names of this structure, reflecting faith in God's help. This name evokes the divine assistance that marked the life of this key figure in Israel's history.
H0499G.emploi: Eleazar appears 63 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the books of Exodus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, which narrate his life and ministry as the priest succeeding Aaron. The Book of Numbers details his administrative and cultic role during the forty years in the desert: he supervises the census of the Levites (Numbers 3), leads military operations with Moses (Numbers 31:21), and participates in major theological decisions such as the inheritance issue of the daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27). The Book of Joshua shows him participating in the distribution of the promised land. The books of Chronicles and Ezra mention him as a direct ancestor of the priestly lineage. Each reference highlights his growing authority and his role as a continuer of Aaron's priestly function.
H0499G.portee: Eleazar embodies the continuity of divine service from one generation to the next: he receives the priesthood from his father and passes it on to his descendants. His life reminds the reader that God preserves and perpetuates His plans through faithful men, even beyond failures or trials. As high priest, he represents the importance of the mediating role in the relationship between God and His people.

sens: son of Abinadab, charged with guarding the ark of the Lord
H0499H.detail: 1. Eleazar is the son of Abinadab, a man from the tribe of Judah. After the ark of the Lord was brought back from the Philistines, it was entrusted to the house of Abinadab, on a hill in Kiriath-Jearim, and Eleazar was consecrated to ensure its care (1 Samuel 7:1). This was a holy responsibility: the ark contained the Tablets of the Law, the very heart of God's presence among Israel.
H0499H.origine: The Hebrew name אֶלְעָזָר (Eleazar) means "God has helped": it is composed of אֵל (El, God) and עָזַר (azar, to help). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in divine help. In the Old Testament, several people bore this name, including the high priest son of Aaron, but also this son of Abinadab mentioned in 1 Samuel 7:1.
H0499H.emploi: Eleazar, son of Abinadab, appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Samuel 7:1. He is briefly mentioned as the man consecrated to guard the ark of the Lord in his father's house at Kiriath-Jearim. This role shows that he received a particular religious distinction, as watching over the ark of the covenant was a serious and holy responsibility.
H0499H.portee: Eleazar reminds us that God chooses ordinary men for extraordinary tasks. Consecrated to a humble yet holy charge, he represents faithfulness in guarding what belongs to God. His story inspires Christians to accept, without fanfare, the responsibilities that the Lord places in their path.

sens: One of David's three mighty warriors
A man of the lineage of Dodo
H0499I.detail:
1. Eleazar is one of the three elite warriors who fought alongside King David against the massed Philistines. While the men of Israel retreated on the heights, Eleazar showed extraordinary courage in battle (2 Samuel 23:9). These three warriors formed an honor guard in the service of the king, recognized for their exceptional strength and bravery.
2. He is the son of Dodo, son of Ahohi, placing Eleazar in a warrior lineage (1 Chronicles 11:12). His name means "God has helped," reflecting the belief that his strength came from divine help rather than from himself alone.
H0499I.origine: The name Eleazar comes from Hebrew where "El" means "God" and "azar" means "to help" or "to rescue." It is a common theophoric name in the Bible, expressing trust in divine help. Several characters bear this name — notably the son of high priest Aaron and other Levitical figures — but in these verses, it specifically refers to the warrior son of Dodo.
H0499I.emploi: Eleazar appears twice in the Bible: in 2 Samuel 23:9 and in 1 Chronicles 11:12, where the same account is reported. He is mentioned among the three most renowned men of David's army, forming an elite warrior group known for their feats in battle. These two passages are nearly identical, underscoring the importance of this character in the military history of the united kingdom under David. The context shows that Eleazar distinguished himself during a major confrontation against the Philistines where he displayed remarkable valor.
H0499I.portee: The account of Eleazar reminds the reader that true courage and strength do not come from oneself, but from God's help — which his name proclaims. It also illustrates how God equips certain men with exceptional abilities for the service of His people and His established king. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that our strengths and victories come from God, not from our personal merit.

sens: Levite, son of Mahli
man without physical descendants
H0499J.detail: 1. Eleazar is a Levite, a member of the tribe of Levi, son of Mahli and brother of Libni and Kish. He is mentioned in the genealogy of the Levites during the time of David and Solomon (1 Chronicles 23:21). 2. He is distinguished by the fact that he had no sons: his daughters married the sons of his brother Kish, thus ensuring a form of family continuity within the tribe (1 Chronicles 23:22 and 24:28).
H0499J.origine: The name "Eleazar" means "God has helped" or "God helps," composed of two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "azar" (to help, to rescue). It is a name of trust that expresses the certainty that God helps His people. The same name designates several other important characters in the history of Israel, including the high priest son of Aaron, but here it refers to a simple Levite from the lineage of Merari.
H0499J.emploi: Eleazar is mentioned three times in the genealogical record of the Levites established during the time of David and Solomon (1 Chronicles 23-24). He belongs to the branch of the sons of Merari, one of the three major Levitical families. Although of modest status — a simple Levite without special priestly charge — he appears in this official list that enumerates the organization of temple service. His particular case, that of a man without sons, is explicitly noted, highlighting the importance of genealogical transmission for Levitical families.

sens: Priest son of Phinehas at the time of the return from exile
H0499K.detail: 1. Eleazar is a priest who appears during the return of the Israelites from exile in Babylon. His name means "God has helped" or "God has aided." He is the son of Phinehas, who is himself a high priest. In Ezra 8:33, he receives and verifies with other Levites the silver, gold, and utensils of the Temple brought from Babylon to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem.
H0499K.origine: The name Eleazar is composed of two Hebrew elements: El (God) and azar (to help, to aid). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the name of God, which is very common in Israel. The meaning of the name reflects a confession of faith: "God has helped." This same name has been borne by several other important figures in the history of Israel, including the high priest son of Aaron and several warriors and Levites.
H0499K.emploi: Eleazar son of Phinehas appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:33. He plays a specific and limited role: to ensure the safe transit of the Temple treasures from Babylon to Jerusalem during the return from exile under the leadership of Ezra, probably in the 5th century B.C. His title of priest and his lineage (son of the high priest Phinehas) guarantee the religious authority and reliability of his function. He is a secondary but important figure in the history of the people who regain their worship.

sens: Man of the tribe of Parosh at the time of the Exile and the return
Name meaning "God has helped"
H0499L.detail:
1. Eleazar is a man of Israel mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:25, among those who had taken foreign wives and had to send them away under the leadership of Ezra. He belongs to the descendants of Parosh, a large family that returned from captivity in Babylon.

2. The name Eleazar means "God has helped" or "God has aided," a name that expresses confidence in divine help — a common characteristic of Hebrew names that proclaim God's actions toward His people at the time of the return from exile.
H0499L.origine: The name Eleazar is formed from two Hebrew elements: "El" (God) and "azar" (to help, to aid). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it. Although other Eleazars appear elsewhere in the Old Testament (the son of Aaron, a soldier of David, a priest at the time of Ezra), this character in Ezra 10:25 is distinct from these other namesakes. The name reflects Israel's faith in God as the one who saves and protects His people.
H0499L.emploi: Eleazar appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:25. He is one of the sons of Parosh who, upon returning from exile in Babylon, had married a foreign woman. Ezra, the scribe and priest, gathered the people, and the men in this situation had to send away their foreign wives to preserve the religious and genealogical purity of Israel. This context shows that the Bible mentions ordinary Israelites, often without further detail, but who participated in major decisions of community reconstruction after the exile.
H0499L.portee: This mention of Eleazar reminds us that the restoration of Israel after the exile was not solely the work of great leaders or famous priests, but also of simple members of the people who accepted the difficult reforms imposed by Ezra. It shows how God worked through the humble and often painful choices of ordinary men to reconstitute His people.

sens: priest who participated in the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem
H0499M.detail: 1. Eleazar is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the dedication ceremony of the restored walls of Jerusalem at the time of Ezra. He is among the singers who celebrated this reconstruction, alongside other priests and Jizrachiah who led them (Nehemiah 12:42).
H0499M.origine: The name Eleazar means "God has helped" or "God has aided," composed of the Hebrew word for God (El) and a root that expresses help or aid. It is a name borne by several men in the history of Israel, including the son of Aaron, high priest of the Old Testament, but this Eleazar is a much later figure, from the time of the reconstruction of the Temple after the exile in Babylon.
H0499M.emploi: This Eleazar is a priest during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, after the return from exile. He is named only once in Nehemiah 12:42, at the time when the restored walls of Jerusalem are solemnly dedicated to God. He appears in a list of priests and singers who participated in this important celebration, showing that he was a man of responsibility in the worship of the restored Temple.

sens: High priest of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H0475M.detail: 1. Eliashib is the high priest (chief priest) who leads the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is a key figure in Israel's return to Jerusalem, and his name appears first in the account of the rebuilding of the Sheep Gate (Nehemiah 3:1). He is so important that his house serves as a geographical landmark in the enumerations of the restored sections (Nehemiah 3:20-21).
H0475M.origine: The name Eliashib means "God restores" or "God reestablishes," composed of the Hebrew word El (God) and a root evoking renewal. It is a highly symbolic name for a high priest who presides over the return and restoration of the temple and the holy city after the Babylonian captivity. This name reflects the messianic hope of the people: God Himself restores His people and their worship.
H0475M.emploi: Eliashib is the high priest of Jerusalem mentioned three times in Nehemiah 3, at the time of the wall reconstruction under Nehemiah (around 445 BC). He is presented as the leader of the priests who participate in the reconstruction work, starting with the Sheep Gate, which leads to the temple. His house and his area of residence serve as spatial reference points to locate the different segments of the wall being repaired. Eliashib represents the religious authority that accompanies Nehemiah's political and religious project.
H0475M.portee: Eliashib embodies the hope of return and restoration. His role as high priest overseeing the rebuilding of the wall shows how the community returned from exile reorganizes around its holy institutions: the temple and its priests. His name itself, "God restores," is a reminder that the renewal of Israel does not come from human strength, but from God's faithfulness and power toward His people.

sens: High priest of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H0475N.detail: Eliashib is a Jewish high priest who lived after the Babylonian exile, at the time when the Israelites returned to Jerusalem. He is the son of Joiakim and the father of Joiada, and is part of the genealogical line of high priests (Nehemiah 12:10). He carries out his priestly duties during the governorship of Nehemiah, under the reign of the Persian king Darius: the chief Levites and priests are officially recorded "in the time of Eliashib" (Nehemiah 12:22). Johanan, son of Eliashib, succeeds him in the priestly ministry (Nehemiah 12:23).
